deep dive S01 · plate 01 of 66 · TASK-SPEC — Title

One bounded task in. One verified attempt out.

This book teaches a single discipline: how to delegate work to a coding agent without ever having to take the agent's word for the result. Task-Spec is the open contract that makes that discipline executable.

The promise on the plate is deliberately narrow. One bounded task in — a task small enough that its entire write surface can be named in advance. One authorized attempt out — a human seals the exact revision of that task before any worker touches it. Portable handoff — the sealed attempt travels as a machine-readable packet, so any conformant executor can pick it up without reinterpretation. And independently verified acceptance — a gate the worker does not control reruns the proof and decides what may close.

The two bold lines underneath are the whole philosophy. No implied authority: if a path, budget, or behavior is not written into the contract, it is not granted. No self-reported done: a worker's claim of completion is an input to verification, never a verdict. Everything in the next sixty-five plates — the schemas, the gates, the graph, the mesh — exists to keep those two sentences true under real delegation.

Read the five tags at the bottom of the plate as the table of contents of the system: bounds, seals, hands off, proves, accepts. Each is a mechanism with its own act in this book, and each returns as a gate you can run from the command line.

How to read the plate
  • The lockup and the question card name the category before any mechanism: this is a contract-and-receipt system, not another agent framework.
  • The five tags are the five promises, in lifecycle order — bound the task, seal the revision, hand off the attempt, prove the behavior, accept the result.
  • The version strip pins what this book describes: Task-Spec v3.9.0, task format v3 by default, MIT-licensed, Bash 3.2+.
Why this page exists

Every later mechanism is judged against this promise. If a feature cannot be traced back to bounding, sealing, handing off, proving, or accepting, it does not belong to the contract.

the claims contract

Claimed precisely.
Refused loudly.

Every claim in this book is bounded by evidence. The left column is what the proof allows; the right column is what this book deliberately refuses. The refusals are a feature, not an apology: a system that names its limits is a system you can audit.

this book may claim
  • One open contract binds scope, behavior, evals, authorization, handoff, and acceptance.
  • Formats 1–4 stay readable; v3 is the authoring default, v4 is opt-in.
  • HMAC v3 detects mutation of the canonical TaskRevision under a shared key.
  • TaskHandoff/v3 binds a portable attempt to revision, authorization, base, closure, scope, and budgets.
  • Independent POST acceptance reruns the proof and validates Git and worktree scope.
  • TaskGraphView/v1 derives the ready frontier and safe concurrency from Markdown and Git.
  • TaskMesh 3.9.0 is an optional local execution control plane over already-authorized leaves.
  • The frozen corridors hold their evidence — 3.8.1 scored 97/100 under its fixed rubric; 3.9.0 retained install, isolation, recovery, cockpit, hosted, provenance, and publication proof.
this book must refuse
  • Universal semantic truth.
  • Ecosystem-wide executor or protocol certification.
  • Long-running production reliability.
  • HMAC as identity, isolation, or semantic correctness.
  • A structural JSON receipt as proof that the claimed real-world behavior occurred.
  • TaskMesh as a hosted service or an authorizer.
  • TaskMesh as a silent replanner or an automatic target-branch merger.
  • A supervised local process as hostile-code isolation.
  • Current-main roster changes as part of the immutable 3.9.0 release corridor.
  • Firecrawl, Tavily, or Exa research as acceptance authority — research may inform authoring only.
If a claim is not on the left, this book does not make it — honesty about limits is the proof posture. SOURCES · [N] brief §2 — the may-claim and must-refuse lists, adapted one-to-one.

the problem · when done is only a claim

Prompts can delegate work.
They cannot define trusted done.

Natural-language intent, the edited repository, and the tests used to judge it can disagree. If the same worker interprets the task and grades the result, a green run may prove only the worker's chosen version of the job.

Underspecified prompts omit requirements that hidden tests enforce and that are not reasonably inferable.

cost · false done

what task-spec changes
Task-Spec separates three authorities: author intent before execution, executor work under a sealed boundary, and independent acceptance after proof. A passing worker claim is evidence to inspect, not authority to close.
Name the two failures first: intent drift and proof overfitting. The third card is the contract boundary: one revision, one authorized attempt, one portable handoff, and independent acceptance. Sources: https://openai.com/index/separating-signal-from-noise-coding-evaluations/; https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16858v3; https://arxiv.org/html/2608.08950v1; README.md; spec/task-spec-v3.md.
deep dive S02 · plate 02 of 66 · THE PROBLEM — When done is only a claim

A green run can be the wrong job, done well.

This page names the disease before the cure: when a task lives only in a chat prompt, “done” is a claim the worker makes about its own work — and nothing in the conversation can falsify it.

The first failure is interpretation drift. Requirements live in prose, and what the prose omits the worker reconstructs from its own priors — so two executors can read the same request and legitimately deliver two different jobs. The quoted OpenAI audit is the measured version of that pain: underspecified prompts omit requirements that hidden tests later enforce and that were never reasonably inferable. The worker did not disobey; the job was never fully said.

The second failure is the self-graded patch. When the same worker interprets the task and judges the result, it optimizes for the checks it can see: visible tests go green while held-out behavior and regression cases quietly break. The run is honestly reported and still a false done — the green proved the worker's chosen version of the job, not the one you meant.

The gold card is the pivot from better prompts to a different object. A Task-Spec leaf keeps behavior, evals, write boundaries, revision, handoff, and acceptance attached to the same authorized attempt — so the task the human meant, the diff the worker wrote, and the proof that ran all name one artifact. The callout underneath names the three separated authorities: author intent before execution, executor work under a sealed boundary, and independent acceptance after proof.

Notice what the fix is not. It is not a longer prompt, and it is not a smarter model. It is a change of authority: a passing worker claim becomes evidence to inspect, not authority to close. Every gate in the rest of this book exists to keep one of these two failure modes from reappearing in a new costume.

How to read the plate
  • The two red cards are cost accounting, not villainy: drift and false done are what prose-only delegation reliably buys.
  • The gold card is the boundary that removes them: one revision, one authorized attempt, one portable handoff, independent acceptance.
  • The pullquote is external evaluation research — the problem is measured, not anecdotal. It informs the framing; it is never an acceptance authority.
  • The bottom callout is the separation the whole book builds on: intent before, sealed work during, acceptance after.
Why this page exists

Every mechanism that follows kills one of these two failure modes. If a later page cannot be traced back to intent drift or self-graded proof, it is ornament — this plate is the test.

Read the center first: it owns bounded contract, executable proof, sealed authority, portable handoff, and independent acceptance. deep dive S03 · plate 03 of 66 · THE CATEGORY — What it is

The thinnest layer that can still say no.

Before any mechanism, this page draws the fence: Task-Spec is the contract layer between what a human wants and what a machine does — and it refuses, on purpose, to be anything more.

Read the center first. Task-Spec owns exactly five things: a bounded contract, executable proof, sealed authority, a portable handoff, and independent acceptance. In one sentence each: the job is written down; the checks are runnable; the exact revision is sealed before work; the attempt travels as a machine-readable packet; and a gate the worker does not control decides what closes. Everything Task-Spec does is one of those five.

Now follow the red rails outward. The prompt stays input — prose carries intent, but it is not the durable authority a worker may close against. The model stays a worker — Task-Spec neither hosts it nor holds provider credentials. The sandbox stays external enforcement — the contract may require environment evidence, but a supervised local process is not a hostile-code boundary. The scheduler may consume the contract — it may never silently rewrite it.

This restraint is load-bearing. If the contract layer also hosted the model, it would be grading its own homework — the exact failure the previous plate named. Keeping every runtime outside means you can swap the prompt tool, the model, the sandbox, or the scheduler without renegotiating the deal: the object in the middle stays portable, diffable, and inspectable.

The bottom line is the epistemic limit. Task-Spec binds what may count as evidence — it does not make weak evidence true, and it does not promise universal semantic truth. A contract can make a claim checkable; it cannot make a bad check wise.

How to read the plate
  • The central plate is the whole product surface — five owned responsibilities, all contract-shaped.
  • The four corner cards are runtimes you bring; the red “not owned” rails terminate at the membrane on purpose.
  • The owns / does-not-own split is the fastest way to debug a misreading of any later page.
  • The verdict strip is the limit: evidence can be bound, never made true.
Why this page exists

Everything after this plate could be misread as an agent framework. This page is the antidote: when a later mechanism looks like orchestration, check the fence — if it is not one of the five owned responsibilities, Task-Spec does not do it.

deep dive S04 · plate 04 of 66 · THE DEVELOPMENT FLOW — From chat to task file

Nothing exists until you say so.

This is the entire onboarding story in one sitting: you describe a change in chat, and a reviewable task file appears — without the agent ever freelancing one into existence.

Watch the left column as five beats. The user asks in one sentence. The Skill Loaded pill flips the session from free-form prompting to the Task-Spec operating loop — from here, the skill drives the CLI. The agent inspects the repository and composes a TaskPlan: one S leaf, two paths, and a preview that answers TASK_PLAN=OK while stressing that no files exist yet. A plan is a proposal, inspectable precisely because it has not happened.

The human's “Approved” is the hard boundary. Only then does the CLI run: batch materializes the approved plan into a task file, validate checks the contract's structure, and definition-of-done checks that every behavior is provable. Each command leaves its own token — TASK_BATCH=OK, VALID, DOD=COMPLETE — so creation itself is an auditable trail, not a side effect of chat.

The lower right window is the artifact those commands produced — below the TaskPlan preview it fulfills. The frontmatter names identity (id, status: ready, format_version: 3), the graph position, the write surface (touches_paths, creates_paths), and the bounded attempt (effort: S, budget_iterations: 15, execution_backend). Below it sit behavior B-1, its eval, and the exit check. The two most important fields are the two that read false: signed_off and accepted.

They stay false because creation never grants authority. The file on disk is a real, validated, complete candidate contract — and it still confers no permission to execute and no verdict of done. Who may flip those two fields is a different question, and it has two different answers.

How to read the plate
  • The chat window is the operating loop, not a transcript: ask → skill loads → plan preview → approve → generate + check.
  • The plan card is the anti-hallucination device: 0 files written means nothing to clean up if the human says no.
  • The run rows are tokens, not vibes — batch, validate, and DoD each report their own result.
  • The lower code window is the generated leaf: frontmatter zones first, then behavior, evaluation, exit check.
The boundary

signed_off: false and accepted: false are the point of the plate. Generation produces a candidate contract; the gates that turn candidate into authorized, and authorized into accepted, come later — and answer different questions.

Receipt
the receipt gate · two different verdicts

PRE says “may run.” POST says “may close.”

Authorization and acceptance are two independent events. One contract crosses both posts. Passing the first never implies the second, and the worker in between holds neither verdict.

PREauthorize · before work

May this run?

Size, structure, traceability, and runnable evals must all pass before the stamp. The stamp seals a TaskRevision, not a filename—edit scope, budget, or dependencies and the seal breaks.

VERDICT · DELEGATE TIER=1|2 · taskspec gate --stamp
WORKexecute · one attempt

One bounded attempt

The worker changes only the handed-off workspace and write surface. It may retry within budget, park with context, and report—it cannot accept itself.

OUTPUT · PATCH + EVIDENCE · one TaskHandoff/v3
POSTaccept · after proof

May this close?

A separate gate reruns the proof and rechecks base commit, closure, blast radius, and evidence against the same authorized attempt. Only its receipt lets status: done exist.

VERDICT · ACCEPTED=1 · taskspec accept --stamp
the rule the deck reuses The two gates answer different questions with different evidence — a green run is a candidate, not a verdict.
Story: this is the mental model the whole deck reuses. Read the five stations left to right. The leaf enters sealed as a TaskRevision. The PRE gate asks only whether it may run: effort, schema, DoD matrix, and runnable evals, then a tier-1 or tier-2 stamp. The attempt is the worker's entire authority: one workspace, one write surface, one budget. The POST gate asks a different question: may this close. It reruns the evals and rechecks base, closure, blast radius, and evidence. Only then does the receipt exist, and only the receipt lets status reach done. Point to the refusal lane: every stop is typed, and a parked attempt is not a failure hidden in chat. Transition: now see the whole loop those two gates sit inside.
deep dive S05 · plate 05 of 66 · THE RECEIPT GATE — Two different verdicts

Permission to start is not permission to finish.

Two decisions guard every delegated task, and they are not the same decision: PRE asks “may this run?” before work begins; POST asks “may this close?” after proof exists.

PRE is authorization, and it happens before any execution. Size, structure, traceability, and runnable evals must all pass; then the stamp seals the exact TaskRevision — the digest of the contract's bytes, not a filename. Edit the scope, the budget, or the dependencies afterward and the seal breaks. The verdict is a named tier — TaskAuthorization/v3 at TIER 1 or 2 — and refusals are typed: INVALID_TASK, DOD_GAPS, TIER_TOO_LOW.

Between the posts sits the worker's entire authority: one attempt, carried as a TaskHandoff/v3, over one workspace and one write surface — touches_paths ∪ creates_paths, nothing else. The worker may retry within budget and may park with context. The one thing it can never do is accept itself.

POST is acceptance, and it belongs to a separate gate the worker does not control. It reruns the proof and re-measures the world — base commit, closure, blast radius, evidence — against the same authorized attempt. Only when all of it holds does the receipt exist: AcceptanceRecord/v1, and only the receipt lets status: done exist. Its refusals are typed too: EVAL_FAILED, BLAST_RADIUS, HANDOFF_STALE.

The two gates answer different questions with different evidence, so passing the first never implies the second — a green run in between is a candidate, not a verdict. This is the mental model the whole book reuses: authorization before work, acceptance after work, and the worker holding neither.

How to read the plate
  • The tall PRE post is the delegation decision; the shorter POST post is the closure decision — different questions, different evidence.
  • The cyan work zone is the portable-contract space: the worker's whole authority is the handoff packet.
  • The red lines under each post are typed refusals — grep-able tokens, never prose.
  • The gold receipt emerges only after POST: authority, recorded.
The boundary

Neither gate claims the code is good in the abstract. PRE certifies the contract is safe to delegate at a named tier; POST certifies this attempt may close. Universal correctness and production reliability stay deliberately out of scope.

Loop
the loop · from intent to accepted

One contract, end to end. Nothing becomes done by narration.

This is the whole life of one task, not only its creation: seven numbered steps from a human intent to an accepted receipt. Each step is one command, and each step leaves a token the next step can check. The two gates from the last slide are steps 04 and 07.

the everyday path · taskspec 3.9.0
# 1–2 · propose, then materialize only what a human approved taskspec plan --manifest tasks/.plans/change.yaml # TASK_PLAN=OK taskspec batch --plan tasks/.plans/change.yaml # approved: true → files # 3–4 · prove the spec, then seal the exact revision taskspec validate tasks/T-leaf.md && taskspec dod tasks/T-leaf.md # DOD=COMPLETE taskspec gate --stamp tasks/T-leaf.md # VERDICT=DELEGATE TIER=1 # 5–6 · hand one attempt to any harness taskspec handoff tasks/T-leaf.md --backend codex --out .taskspec/handoffs/a1.json # … executor works inside the handed-off boundary … # 7 · an independent gate reruns the proof and closes taskspec accept --handoff .taskspec/handoffs/a1.json --stamp tasks/T-leaf.md # ACCEPTED=1
who does what on the loop
humanapproves the plan · holds the signing key · reads the receipt
taskspecvalidates, stamps, packages, reruns, and records
executoredits only inside write_surface · reports pass / retry / park
neverthe executor marking its own task done
exit codes0 ok · 1 gate/contract failure · 2 usage · 3 runtime
the preview The rest of the deck opens each station in turn — the leaf, the plan, the seal, the packet, the proof, the receipt — and the loop never changes shape.
Story: do not teach each mechanism yet. Walk the seven stations once so the audience has the whole shape. Plan proposes a topology and writes nothing; batch materializes only what a human approved, so the second chip is the first place human authority enters. Validate and DoD ask whether the spec is provable, not whether the feature exists. Gate stamps the exact revision: that is PRE from the previous slide. Handoff is the portable packet any harness can pick up. Execute is the only station the worker owns. Accept is POST: it reruns the proof and writes the receipt that lets status reach done. Then point at the trail: every station leaves a token. The code window is the real everyday path from the demo. The panel answers the question people are already forming: who does what. deep dive S06 · plate 06 of 66 · THE LOOP — From intent to accepted

Seven stations, and none of them is “trust me.”

Here is the entire life of one task as seven commands — the map this book enlarges, one station at a time, from a sentence of intent to an accepted receipt.

Stations one to three create the contract. plan proposes the topology and writes nothing. batch materializes only what a human approved — the HUMAN APPROVED chip is the first place authority enters. validate + dod ask whether the spec is provable, not whether the feature exists yet. Their tokens — TASK_PLAN=OK, DOD=COMPLETE — are the trail that creation leaves behind.

Station four is the PRE gate from the last plate: gate --stamp seals the exact revision and answers TIER=1. Station five packages one portable attempt as TaskHandoff/v3 — a packet any harness can pick up without reinterpretation. Station six is the only station the worker owns: execute inside the handed-off boundary and report EVAL=PASS.

Station seven is POST: accept --stamp reruns the proof and stamps the receipt — ACCEPTED=1 — and only now may status reach done. The rail's rule gives the plate its title: nothing becomes done by narration. Every state crossing is a checkable token; a chat message is never one.

The panel answers the question forming in your head. The human approves the plan, holds the signing key, and reads the receipt. The CLI validates, stamps, packages, reruns, and records. The executor edits only inside write_surface and reports pass, retry, or park. And the refused row is the whole point: the executor never marks its own task done. The bash window is the real everyday path from the demo — tests/test-demo.sh keeps it honest, down to the exit codes.

How to read the plate
  • The chips above the rail name the state crossing each boundary; the token trail below names the artifact that proves it.
  • Stations 04 and 07 are the PRE and POST gates from the receipt-gate plate — the same two questions, now in context.
  • The bash window is the runnable demo path, not an illustration.
  • The exit-code row is a contract too: 0 ok, 1 gate/contract failure, 2 usage, 3 runtime.
Why this page exists

A reader who can retell these seven stations can place every mechanism that follows — the leaf, the plan, the seal, the packet, the proof, the receipt. This page is the map; the rest of the book walks the territory.

Roles
the authority · who may decide

Four roles. No one issues authority to itself.

The loop works because the powers are split. An author proposes, a human authorizes, an executor works, an independent gate accepts — and every grant of authority crosses a boundary as a signed object, never as a promise inside one actor’s head.

why this matters One person can wear several hats on a small repo — but the objects still cross the boundaries, so the trail reads the same at any team size.
Story: the chat slide showed one person and one agent; this slide names the four hats that were actually in play. Walk the arrows in order. One: the author — often the agent itself — proposes a plan; proposing grants nothing. Two: the human authorizer approves the topology and stamps the seal; this is the only place a signing key exists. Three: the executor returns a patch and evidence; it worked inside the handoff and cannot widen it. Four: the acceptor answers with a receipt or a typed refusal back to the human. Then point at the red loop: the executor checking its own work and declaring done is the exact arrow prompt-based delegation relies on, and the one this system refuses. Close with the footer: on a solo repo you wear all four hats, but the objects still cross the boundaries, so the audit trail is identical. Transition: with the roles clear, open the object they pass between them — the leaf itself. Sources: OPERATING.md; src/author/; src/gate/; src/dispatch/; src/accept/.
deep dive S07 · plate 07 of 66 · THE AUTHORITY — Who may decide

Nobody grades their own exam.

Four powers move a task from idea to accepted — proposing, authorizing, executing, accepting — and this page puts each in a different pair of hands.

Walk the gold rails in order. One: the author — often the agent itself — sends the TaskPlan/v1 and the atomic leaf to the human; proposing grants nothing. Two: the authorizer approves the topology and stamps the seal, and out go TaskAuthorization/v3 and TaskHandoff/v3 — this lane holds the only signing key, and it never hands that key to a model. Three: the executor works inside the handoff and returns the patch plus attempt evidence; it cannot widen what it was given. Four: the acceptor reruns the proof and answers with AcceptanceRecord/v1 — or a typed refusal — back to the human.

The red crossed loop is the argument of the whole book in one glyph. “I checked my own work — it's done” is the arrow prompt-based delegation relies on, and it is the one arrow this system refuses to draw. Every other arrow is a signed, inspectable object — which is why the rails are gold: what crosses a boundary here is authority, or a receipt of authority, never a promise inside one actor's head.

Because each crossing is an artifact, accountability becomes data rather than chat history. Months later you can list the plans, diff the authorizations, replay the handoffs, and audit the receipts — the conversation can vanish and the trail survives.

One person can wear several hats. On a solo repo the author and the authorizer may be the same human, and that is fine: the system does not require a large team, it requires that the objects still cross the boundaries, so the trail reads the same at any size. And the symmetry matters too — human authority is explicit here without every technical gate becoming manual; validate, handoff, and accept all run as commands.

How to read the plate
  • The four lanes are powers, not job titles: propose, authorize, execute, accept.
  • The gold rails are the only connections — every grant of authority crosses as a signed object.
  • Each lane's red line names what that role may never do; the executor's is the one the diagram dramatizes.
  • The footer is the scaling story: hats can combine; boundaries cannot.
Key detail

The authorizer lane holds the only key. Automation is welcome everywhere else, but sealing a revision stays a human-answerable decision — that is what “no self-issued authority” means in practice.

deep dive S08 · plate 08 of 66 · THE ANATOMY — One leaf, six zones

A file a validator can read, zone by zone.

A Task-Spec leaf is one Markdown file with a strict two-part anatomy: a YAML frontmatter cap that says who the task is and what state it is in, and six numbered zones below it that carry everything an executor — human or machine — needs to do the work and prove it.

The split is deliberate. The cap holds identity and lifecycle — fields like id, status, effort, the two path lists, and the envelope flags signed_off and accepted. Those authority-bearing fields are exactly what later gets sealed into the TaskRevision digest, so the top of the file stays small, typed, and stable. Everything the executor must do lives below the fence, written as prose a human reviews, under headings a script can find.

Each zone answers one question. Intent: why does this task deserve to exist? Behavior: what must become true? Contract: can a script tell real work from a stub — this is the moat, home of the runnable success criteria, the Validation Card, and the Exit Check. Guardrails: what must never happen? Operations: what is still open or assumed, surfaced here instead of silently shaping the code? Reversal & Runtime: how do we undo the change and watch it live — required only in the full profile, because rigor scales with blast radius.

Why zones instead of one fluent prompt? Because separated zones make validation mechanical. A paragraph mixes goal, scope, and proof into one blob; a validator cannot check a vibe. With named zones, a gate can ask “does the Behavior zone hold at least one B-N?” and “does every eval in the Contract zone name a behavior it verifies?” — and get yes/no answers straight from the file. The next nine plates put each band under a lamp; this map is the reference they all return to.

How to read the plate
  • The silver cap is the frontmatter — who, where, what state; its authority-bearing fields are what the seal later binds into the revision digest.
  • Each colored band is one zone, labeled by the question it answers, not just a name.
  • Zone 3 sits in green and is called the moat: runnable proof that separates real work from a stub.
  • Zone 6 is marked full-profile only — reversal and observability appear where blast radius justifies them.
Why this page exists

Before any single field can mean anything, the reader needs a stable map of the whole artifact. The six-zone anatomy is that map: profiles, traceability, and the Validation Card are each one of these bands examined up close. Where older documents use different zone names, the normative v3 structure governs.

Identity: which task, what state, which format. Graph: dependencies decide readiness, not vibes. Write surface: the two path lists that acceptance will later compare against the real diff. Runtime and budget: effort tier, iteration budget, backend. Then family five, full width and green: the PRE and POST envelopes. deep dive S09 · plate 09 of 66 · THE FRONTMATTER — Accountability is data

Everything the chat forgets, the cap remembers.

The frontmatter is the leaf's machine-readable face: five families of typed fields that answer who, where, how big, on what — and who authorized and accepted it — without anyone scrolling back through a conversation.

The first four families describe the task. Identity pins id, status, format_version, and profile. Graph fields — depends_on, parent, supersedes — place the leaf in the plan; status: ready means every dependency is already done, not that someone feels good about it. The write surface lists the only paths the task may change, and acceptance will later compare the real diff against exactly those two lists. Runtime & budget — effort, budget_iterations, execution_backend — bounds how large the attempt may grow and where it runs. Nothing here is prose: every field is typed so a script, not a reader's memory, carries the answer.

The fifth family is different in kind: signed_off and accepted are machine-stamped only, which is why that card spans the full width in green. The vocabulary matters — authorization happens before work, acceptance after it, and the two are never the same gate. Only the PRE stamp and the POST stamp may write here. A hand edit does not merely look wrong: it changes the sealed TaskRevision, breaks the digest match, and drops the task's trust to Tier 3.

Under the window, the lifecycle strip draws status as a state machine — ready, in-progress, blocked, parked, done — with one rule that gives the word “done” its meaning: the only edge into it runs through a gold lock labeled accepted: true, and the transition tool refuses every other route. Blocked and parked always return through ready; there is no side door back into work. That is the plate's closing line in practice: accountability is data, and grep can answer “who authorized this, and when?” long after the conversation is gone.

How to read the plate
  • The comment rules in the window split the cap into the five families on the right — read it top to bottom.
  • Family five spans full width in green: the two envelopes no human may edit.
  • The lifecycle strip is the same status field drawn as a state machine, gold lock included.
  • Blocked and parked loop back through ready — there is no side door into done.
Key detail

The cap stays small on purpose: every authority-bearing field in it is sealed into the TaskRevision digest at the PRE gate. The fewer moving parts above the fence, the stronger the seal's meaning below it.

Size
the effort gate · leaf or node

XS to L execute. XL and XXL only compose.

Size is not an estimate — it is a permission. Four tiers may be handed to an executor, each with a hard cap on how many paths it may write. Anything larger is a composition node: it holds children, owns no write surface, and can never be delegated whole.

why a hard cap A small write surface keeps the blast radius checkable — the validator enforces these caps mechanically, so “too big to review” never reaches an executor.
Story: size is a permission, not an estimate. Walk the ruler left to right. XS through M are ordinary leaves with write caps of one, two, and three paths — small enough that acceptance can compare the real diff against the declared surface. L is still a leaf but glows gold: up to five paths, one coherent done-condition, and only on a backend configured for long-horizon work (TASKSPEC_LONG_HORIZON_BACKENDS). Then the dashed frames: XL needs at least two children, XXL at least three, and nodes can nest — tasks all the way down. They own no write surface, so handing one to an executor is refused, not discouraged. Close on the italic line: the gate does not forbid ambition; it forces decomposition until every piece is individually checkable. Transition: size controls breadth; profile controls proof depth — that is the next slide. Sources: spec/task-spec-v3.md (six-tier effort contract); src/lib/_lib.sh ts_size_writes_max (XS=1 S=2 M=3 L=5) and ts_size_min_children (XL≥2 XXL≥3); src/gate/validate-task-spec.sh check 3; tests/test-effort-sizing.sh.
deep dive S10 · plate 10 of 66 · THE EFFORT GATE — Leaf or node

Too big to review never reaches the runner.

Effort is not a guess about how long a task feels — it is a permission that decides whether a task may be handed to an executor at all, and how many paths it may write.

Four sizes are executable leaves. XS, S, and M are ordinary units of work with hard write-surface caps of one, two, and three paths. L is a long-horizon leaf: up to five paths and one coherent done-condition, and only on a backend configured for long-horizon work. The caps exist so acceptance can compare the entire real diff against the declared surface without a reviewer holding the whole change in their head. Note the direction of the rule: bigger tasks get more scrutiny, never more reach.

XL and XXL are a different species: composition nodes. They own no write surface at all — zero paths — and exist only to hold children: at least two for XL, at least three for XXL, and nodes may nest, tasks all the way down. The plate draws them as dashed containers rather than solid cards precisely because you can see the child leaves inside. And because there is nothing an executor could safely write, handing one over is not discouraged; the validator refuses it, mechanically, every time.

This is the atomicity guard, and it is what makes the next act's graph possible: large ambitions are not forbidden — they are decomposed until every piece fits through the gate as an individually checkable leaf. The ruler on the plate is enforced, not aspirational; the same size-to-cap table lives in the validation script and its tests, so “too big to review” can never reach a worker disguised as a single task. Size is the first gate a task passes — before profiles, before evals, before any executor sees it.

How to read the plate
  • Solid cards are executable leaves; dashed frames are composition nodes with child leaves inside.
  • The ruler under each size states its write cap and its handoff verdict — yes, capable-backend-only, or refused.
  • L glows gold: still a leaf, but gated on a long-horizon-capable backend.
  • The nested XL chip inside XXL shows that nodes compose — children can themselves be nodes.
The boundary

The refusal is the feature. A gate that merely warns about oversized work moves the argument to code review, where it is lost; a gate that refuses forces decomposition while it is still cheap — at authoring time.

Story: the previous slide capped breadth; this one scales depth. Read the towers left to right as sediment: lite is the floor every leaf must have — a goal and the three proof sections; behavior is implied by the evals. Standard is the default (an absent profile field resolves to standard): it adds the Behavior zone with given/when/then scenarios, context, guardrails, and open questions, and turns on the load-bearing rule — every behavior verified by at least one eval, every eval naming the behavior it verifies. Full is for work nobody watches: unattended dispatch, hard-to-reverse changes, security or financial-critical severity; it demands a Rollback Plan and Observability Hooks, with a literal "(none — additive)" allowed when rollback truly does not apply. Close on the invariant: profile never expands write authority. Transition: regardless of profile, the leaf begins with observable behavior — write the behavior before the patch. deep dive S11 · plate 11 of 66 · THE PROFILES — Proof scales with risk

The file must answer for itself when nobody is watching.

Effort capped how much a leaf may touch; profile decides how much it must prove — three named tiers of required depth, enforced by the validator zone by zone.

Lite is the minimum valid leaf: a Goal plus the three proof sections — Success Criteria, Validation Card, Exit Check. Behavior is implied by the evals, acceptable only for narrow, low-risk work where the check says everything that matters. Standard is the everyday default — an absent profile field resolves to it — and adds the sections that make a leaf legible to another person: explicit B-N behaviors in given/when/then form, context, anti-patterns and do-not-touch paths, and open questions. Each card on the plate is drawn as the document itself: dimmed sections are inherited from the tier below, bright sections are what the tier adds — the towers grow by accumulation.

Standard also switches on this act's load-bearing rule: bidirectional traceability — every behavior verified by at least one eval, every eval naming the behavior it verifies. That is the cyan token at the foot of the middle card, and all of plate S15 is devoted to it. Full is the unattended tier, for work that runs unwatched, is hard to reverse, or carries security- or financial-critical severity: it demands zone 6 — a Rollback Plan and Observability Hooks — with a literal “(none — additive)” permitted when rollback genuinely does not apply.

The red rail at the bottom states the invariant that keeps profiles honest: profile changes required proof depth; it never expands write authority. A full-profile leaf still writes only its declared paths. Rigor is a floor scaled to what the work can break — never a privilege that lets a riskier task reach further than a tiny one. Pick the tier by what a mistake would cost, and the validator holds that line zone by zone.

How to read the plate
  • Each card is a miniature document; dim sections are inherited, bright ones are added at that tier.
  • The “adds” separators make the accumulation explicit — standard includes lite, full includes standard.
  • Card height is the message: proof depth grows with risk, not with size.
  • The red invariant rail is a boundary: depth scales, write authority does not.
Why this page exists

Profiles keep the format usable. Without them, either every typo fix carries a rollback plan and nobody uses the format, or every unattended financial task ships on a vibe and nobody trusts it. Three named tiers let the validator enforce the difference by name.

SOURCES · [N] normative: spec/task-spec-v3.md — [D] docs/concepts/profiles.md. “Regardless of profile, the leaf begins with observable behavior” — next: the behavior.
B-1
the behavior · given / when / then

Write the behavior before the patch.

Success is an observable state transition, not a to-do list. B-1 from the CSV-export leaf names a starting state, one action, and a checkable outcome — which is exactly what lets a script judge it later.

B-1
given · the starting state
a payments report with rows
A state a test can set up on demand — seed the report, no humans required.
reproducible
one action
▶
when · the trigger
the user requests CSV export
A single action at a real boundary — a command, a call, a click — not an internal step.
one trigger
the world changes
✓
then · the observable outcome
a CSV with the same rows exists
A fact the machine can check: the file exists and its rows match. True or false, no opinion.
checkable · deterministic
the anti-card · implementation narration
“Refactor the exporter, improve the report module, add a helper.”
Every item narrates the patch, not the world. A stub can satisfy all three, nothing here can fail on purpose, and “done” becomes a matter of opinion again.
NOT SETTABLENOT CHECKABLEA STUB PASSES
why this shape matters
Because B-1 names an observable transition, the eval that claims it — eval_1 (verifies B-1) — can fail on the unpatched repo and pass on the patch. The behavior is what gives the proof something to discriminate.
the honest limit
Given/when/then does not replace design judgment — it only guarantees that whatever you decided is stated as something the world can verify.
the test Read your behavior and ask: could a stub pass it? If yes, it narrates the patch — rewrite it until the world, not the code, is what changed.
Story: this opens the proof act. Walk the three cards: given is a state a test can set up on demand; when is one action at a real boundary; then is a fact the machine can check without opinion. Use the CSV leaf so the audience recognizes B-1 from the anatomy slide. Then the red card: implementation narration — refactor, improve, add a helper — describes the patch instead of the world. Nothing there can fail on purpose, so a stub passes and done becomes opinion again; this is the S02 problem sneaking back in through task wording. The green callout lands the connection: eval_1 verifies B-1, and only an observable transition lets that eval fail before the patch and pass after. The gold callout keeps it honest: this does not replace design judgment. Close on the footer test: could a stub pass it? Transition: behavior says what must be true; contract says where the worker may make it true — the write surface is next. Sources: spec/task-spec-v3.md (Zone 2, traceability rule); docs/concepts/eval-driven-development.md; docs/concepts/edd-vs-sdd-honest-comparison.md.
deep dive S12 · plate 12 of 66 · THE BEHAVIOR — Given / when / then

If a stub can pass it, it was never a behavior.

A behavior is a promise about the world, written before any code exists: GIVEN a starting state, WHEN one action happens, THEN an observable fact holds — stated so a script can judge it.

Each clause carries a discipline. Given must be a state a test can set up on demand — seed the report, no humans required. When must be a single action at a real boundary — a command, a call, a click — never an internal implementation step. Then must be a fact the machine can check without opinion: the file exists, its rows match, true or false. The plate's B-1 is the CSV-export leaf's promise, and it satisfies all three.

The red anti-card shows the failure mode: implementation narration. “Refactor the exporter, improve the report module, add a helper” describes the patch, not the world. Nothing in it can fail on purpose, a stub satisfies all three items, and “done” collapses back into opinion — the exact problem this contract exists to kill. The plate's self-test is one question: could a stub pass this? If yes, rewrite until the world, not the code, is what changed.

The payoff lands three plates later: because B-1 names an observable transition, the eval that claims it — eval_1 (verifies: B-1) — can fail on the unpatched repo and pass on the patch. That discriminating property gives the proof something to prove; a check that cannot tell baseline from candidate is theater. This is eval-driven development introduced honestly — the behavior is written first so the check has something to discriminate, with no claim that the technique decides what to build. And the honest limit matters: given/when/then does not replace design judgment — it only guarantees that whatever you decided is stated as something the world can verify.

How to read the plate
  • The three nodes flow left to right: state, trigger, outcome — gold to cyan to green.
  • The green THEN node is a gate: checkable and deterministic, or the behavior is not finished being written.
  • The red anti-card is deliberately the same shape — narration wears the costume of a behavior.
  • The two callouts are the connection and the caveat: discrimination for the eval, no replacement for judgment.
The honest limit

Eval-driven development here is a discipline of statement, not a claim of universal truth: a behavior can be perfectly checkable and still be the wrong thing to build. Design judgment stays human; the contract only makes the decision verifiable.

Moat
the contract · where work may land

The write surface is a set, not a vibe.

The executor can see the whole repository — it may write only inside the declared set: existing files go in touches_paths, new files in creates_paths. Everything else is outside its authority.

why a set Sets can be compared by a machine — at acceptance, observed paths ⊆ declared paths is a computation, not a code-review argument.
Story: behavior said what must become true; this says where it may happen. Point at the frame first: the executor reads everything — context is free. Then the moat: two declared paths, and the distinction matters — payments.py exists today so it is touches; the test does not exist yet so it is creates, and the validator refuses an entry in the wrong list. Then the three refused arrows: billing is guarded by do-not-touch; secrets are simply outside the set; .git is protected, and symlink tricks are resolved to real paths before checking. The docs arrow makes the quietest rule explicit: docs is not forbidden by name — it is simply undeclared, and undeclared is enough to refuse. Close on the caption: the boundary is enforced twice, during the attempt and again at acceptance from the real Git diff — that second check is the blast-radius slide later. Transition: allowed paths define the moat; guardrails define behavior inside it. Sources: spec/task-spec-v3.md; src/lib/workspace.py; src/accept/preflight.py; docs/patterns/do-not-touch-detection.md.
deep dive S13 · plate 13 of 66 · THE CONTRACT — The write surface

Read everything. Write almost nothing.

The write surface is the set of paths a leaf may change — write_surface = touches_paths ∪ creates_paths — and because it is a set, enforcing it is a computation, not a code-review argument.

The executor may read the whole repository; context is free. It may write only inside the declared set, and the split matters: existing files belong in touches_paths, files that do not exist yet belong in creates_paths, and the validator refuses an entry filed in the wrong list. The plate's payments.py exists today, so it is a touch; the test file does not, so it is a create. The plate draws this as a moat for a reason: a blacklist enumerates what is forbidden and inevitably forgets something; a declared set enumerates what is allowed and refuses everything else by default.

The four refused arrows are the four ways a write can fall outside authority. src/billing/ is guarded by name through the do-not-touch list. secrets/.env never enters a task at all. .git/ is protected — history is evidence, not workspace — and symlink tricks are resolved to real paths before the check. The quietest rule is docs/: not forbidden by name, simply undeclared — and undeclared is enough to refuse. Authority is granted by listing, never assumed.

And the boundary is checked twice: refused during the attempt, then re-measured from the real Git diff at acceptance, where observed paths must be a subset of declared paths. That second measurement is what makes blast-radius acceptance possible later in the book — the acceptor does not trust what the task said it would touch; it recomputes what the attempt actually touched and compares the two sets. Two lists, written before the work starts, are the entire permission model — small enough to review at a glance, strict enough to enforce without one.

How to read the plate
  • The faint outer frame is the whole repository — readable; the luminous cyan moat is the only writable region.
  • Cyan card: an existing file under touches_paths; green card: a new file under creates_paths.
  • Each red refusal node carries a typed label — DO-NOT-TOUCH, OUT_OF_SURFACE, PROTECTED, UNDECLARED.
  • The caption states the double check — refused mid-attempt, re-measured from the diff at acceptance.
The boundary

Everything outside the set is outside authority — including paths nobody thought to forbid. “Undeclared is enough to refuse” is what turns a permission list into a moat instead of a blacklist.

Rails
the guardrails · what must not happen

Failure is designed, not suffered.

The leaf does not only say what to build — it says what must never happen, when to stop trying, and how to undo and observe the result. Three rails, one for each moment of the attempt.

01
prevent
Named forbidden moves

stop
Budgets end the attempt
Retries are bounded twice: a hard iteration budget and a no-progress circuit breaker. When either trips, the attempt parks — with its context attached.
budget_iterations: 15 no_progress_breaker: 3 on_terminal_failure: park_with_context
no infinite loops · no silent thrash

recover
Undo is written first
The full profile demands a rollback plan and observability hooks before the work starts — how to reverse it, and where to watch it live.

reversal scales with blast radius
the reframe A parked task with its context attached beats a confident mess — stopping well is a feature of the contract, not an agent surprise.
Story: the moat said where; guardrails say how the attempt is allowed to behave inside it. Walk the rail: before, during, after. Prevent: anti-patterns and do-not-touch are named in the file — reordering report columns is the CSV example of a change that passes tests and still breaks a consumer; billing is the neighbor nobody may touch. These are not advice: acceptance checks them. Stop: two independent brakes — a hard iteration budget (15 on our leaf) and a no-progress circuit breaker (three tries without the eval getting closer), and the terminal behavior is itself declared: park with context, so the next attempt starts from evidence instead of zero. Recover: full profile demands the undo and the watchpoint before work starts; reversal rigor scales with blast radius. Close on the reframe: stopping well is a designed outcome. Transition: a behavior is only operational when a runnable check points back to it — traceability is next. deep dive S14 · plate 14 of 66 · THE GUARDRAILS — What must not happen

Stopping well is a feature, not a surprise.

Guardrails make refusal part of the contract: the leaf states what must never happen, when the attempt must stop trying, and how to undo and observe the result — all before any work begins.

The three rails follow the attempt's timeline. Prevent (before): anti-patterns and do-not-touch paths are named in the file — “do not reorder report columns” is the CSV example of a change that passes every test and still breaks a consumer. These are not advice; acceptance checks them. Stop (during): two independent brakes — a hard budget_iterations cap and a circuit_breaker_no_progress trip — and the terminal behavior is itself declared: on_terminal_failure: park_with_context. No infinite loops, no silent thrash — the attempt ends by rule, not by someone noticing the bill.

Recover (after): the full profile demands the undo and the watchpoint up front — a Rollback Plan and Observability Hooks — scaled to blast radius, because a change nobody can reverse or see is a change nobody should delegate. This is why zone 6 appears only in the full profile: reversal rigor grows with what the work can break. The plate's chips are literal file content — section names and field values, not paraphrase.

The reframe is the plate's point. A stopped attempt is not a failed contract; it is the contract working. Parking with its context attached means the next attempt — human or machine — starts from evidence instead of zero: what was tried, what the evals said, why the brakes fired. A parked task with context beats a confident mess every time. And these numbers are not prose wishes: two plates later they reappear inside the Validation Card as machine-readable fields every harness obeys. Stopping well is a designed outcome, not an agent surprise. None of this prevents failure; it makes failure legible, bounded, and reversible by construction.

How to read the plate
  • The gradient rail maps the attempt's timeline: before (red, refuse), during (gold, stop), after (green, undo & see).
  • Prevent names the forbidden moves — anti-patterns and do-not-touch paths, checked at acceptance, not on trust.
  • Stop's numbers — 15 iterations, 3 no-progress tries, park_with_context — are the same fields the Validation Card carries.
  • Recover is labeled full-profile: rollback and observability scale with blast radius.
Why this page exists

Agents surprise their operators mostly by not stopping. Making stopping a designed, declared outcome — budgets, a circuit breaker, and a parked-with-context terminal state — removes the surprise without removing the attempt.

Witness
the traceability · behavior ↔ eval

No orphan behavior. No unexplained eval.

Every promise must have a witness, and every check must say what it is checking. The DoD gate walks this graph mechanically — a single unclaimed line on either side blocks the seal.

the load-bearing rule Fix both red items — give B-4 a measurable witness or delete it, name what eval_x verifies or drop it — and the same graph returns DOD=COMPLETE.
Story: this is the rule that makes DOD=COMPLETE mean something. Left column is zone 2, the promises; right column is zone 3, the proof. Walk the healthy lines first: eval_1 claims B-1 and B-2 by name in its verifies list; eval_2 is the terminal witness — the whole Exit Check as one command — and claims B-3. Then the two failures. B-4 is an orphan: "feels fast" has no witness because as written nothing can measure it; the gate does not argue taste, it refuses the graph. eval_x is the mirror image: a green check that answers no promise is noise, and noise is how Goodharting starts. Both directions are enforced — no orphan behavior, no unexplained eval — and the verdict chip shows the consequence: DOD=GAPS blocks the seal, so this graph literally stands between the leaf and the PRE gate. Close on the footer: two small edits and the same graph goes green. Transition: the witnesses exist — the Validation Card tells the runner how they behave: run, retry, emit. Sources: spec/task-spec-v3.md (traceability rule); src/gate/definition-of-done.sh; docs/concepts/profiles.md.
deep dive S15 · plate 15 of 66 · THE TRACEABILITY — Behavior to eval

Every promise needs a witness — and every witness a promise.

Traceability is a bidirectional rule: no behavior may exist without an eval that verifies it, and no eval may exist without naming the behavior it verifies — and a gate walks that graph mechanically.

Read the healthy lines first. eval_1 claims [B-1, B-2] by name in its verifies list; eval_2 is marked terminal — the whole Exit Check run as one command — and claims [B-3]. The cyan witness lines make the claiming visible: promises on the left, proof on the right, every edge declared in the file where a script can walk it. Many-to-one is fine — one eval may witness several behaviors; what is forbidden is a zero on either side.

The two red items are the two failure directions. B-4 — “the export should feel fast” — is an orphan behavior: as written, nothing can measure it, so no eval can honestly claim it. The gate does not argue taste; it refuses the graph. eval_x is the mirror image, an unexplained eval: a green check with verifies: [] that answers no promise. Unexplained green is noise, and noise is where Goodharting starts — a suite full of checks that prove nothing still looks like proof. Each direction kills a different lie: orphans hide unverifiable wishes, unexplained evals hide theater.

The consequence is the verdict chip: DOD=GAPS, and the seal is blocked — this graph stands between the leaf and the PRE gate. The fix is deliberately small: give B-4 a measurable witness or delete it; name what eval_x verifies or drop it. Make those two edits and the same graph returns DOD=COMPLETE. That is what “complete” means when the Definition-of-Done gate runs: not “the suite is green,” but “every promise has a witness and every witness has a promise.” Both directions, every time, or the seal does not happen.

How to read the plate
  • Left column is zone 2, what must become true; right column is zone 3, what proves it.
  • Solid cyan lines are declared witnesses; arrowheads land on the claiming eval.
  • Red cards fail in opposite directions: a promise with no witness, a witness with no promise.
  • The verdict chip is literal gate output — DOD=GAPS blocks the seal until both red items are fixed.
Key detail

The rule runs both ways because each direction catches a different failure. Orphan behaviors hide unverifiable wishes inside the spec; unexplained evals hide ceremonial green inside the suite. Completeness requires neither.

Card
the validation card · run, retry, emit

The execution contract for the proof itself.

The witnesses exist — this card tells any harness how they behave: how each check runs, when to stop retrying, and which machine states the worker may report. It is why the same leaf runs on Codex, Claude Code, or Kimi without translation.

## Validation Card · tasks/T-20260826-payments-csv-export.md
# ── run ─ how each witness executes success_criteria: - id: eval_1 runnable: bash check_type: deterministic verifies: [B-1, B-2] - id: eval_2 runnable: bash terminal: true verifies: [B-3] # ── retry ─ when the loop must stop retry_policy: max_iterations: 15 circuit_breaker_no_progress: 3 on_terminal_failure: park_with_context # ── contract ─ what any executor reads, produces, and may say agent_contract: version: 2 sandbox_type: workspace-write timeout_minutes: 30 read: [intent, behavior, contract, guardrails] produce: [code, tests] emit: [pass, fail, retry_with_reason, parked_with_context]

How does this check execute, and what does it claim?
runnable names the interpreter, check_type the kind of judgment, verifies the promises it claims — and one eval is terminal: the whole Exit Check as a single command.
RETRYThe loop has brakes built in
How long may the worker keep trying?
The guardrail numbers from two slides ago live here, machine-readable: 15 iterations, 3 no-progress tries, then park_with_context — the same values every harness obeys.
EMITFour words, no prose
What may the worker say back?
pass · fail · retry_with_reason · parked_with_context — machine states, not paragraphs. Notice what is missing: there is no “done” in the executor’s vocabulary.
the payoff Intent, proof, and stopping rules travel inside the file — swap the harness and nothing about the job changes.
Story: the traceability graph said which witness claims which promise; this card says how those witnesses behave at runtime. Walk the three blocks by their comments. Run: every eval is typed — runnable names the interpreter, check_type the kind of judgment, verifies the claims — and eval_2 is terminal, the whole Exit Check as one command. Retry: the guardrail numbers from the stop card are not advice in prose, they are fields any harness reads: fifteen iterations, three no-progress tries, park with context. Contract: agent_contract is schema-versioned (v2 only), declares the sandbox type and timeout, what the executor must read on pickup, what it may produce, and the only four states it may emit. Land the punchline on emit: pass, fail, retry_with_reason, parked_with_context — "done" is not in the vocabulary, which is the whole deck in one field. Close on the payoff: this is why the same leaf runs on any harness without translation. deep dive S16 · plate 16 of 66 · THE VALIDATION CARD — Run, retry, emit

The worker may say four words — and “done” is not one of them.

The Validation Card is the execution contract for the proof itself: it tells any harness how each check runs, when the retry loop must stop, and which machine states the worker may report — so the same leaf runs on Codex, Claude Code, or Kimi without translation.

Run: every eval is typed. runnable names the interpreter, check_type the kind of judgment, verifies the promises it claims — the traceability graph made executable. One eval is terminal: true: the entire Exit Check as a single command, the decisive witness whose green ends the attempt. The three comment rules in the window — run, retry, contract — are mirrored one-to-one by the cards on the right.

Retry: the stopping rules from the guardrails plate reappear here as fields, not prose — max_iterations, circuit_breaker_no_progress, on_terminal_failure: park_with_context. Because they are machine-readable, every harness applies the same brakes to the same leaf, and a parked attempt carries its context to whoever picks it up next.

Contract: agent_contract is schema-versioned (version: 2) and declares the sandbox type, the timeout, what the executor must read on pickup, what it may produce, and the only four states it may emit: pass, fail, retry_with_reason, parked_with_context. Machine states, not paragraphs. Notice what is missing from the vocabulary: there is no “done.” The worker reports evidence; acceptance — a gate the worker does not control — decides what may close.

This is the portability mechanism the book promised at the start: intent, proof, and stopping rules travel inside the file, runtime-neutral by construction. Swap the harness and nothing about the job changes. The claim stays deliberately bounded — a conformant executor knows what to run and what it may say; the card does not certify what any runtime does beyond that boundary.

How to read the plate
  • The window's three comment rules — run, retry, contract — map one-to-one to the cards on the right.
  • verifies: [B-1, B-2] is the same claim the traceability plate drew as a cyan line.
  • The emit list is the punchline: four machine states, none of them “done.”
  • sandbox_type and timeout_minutes bound the attempt's environment in the same block.
The boundary

The card makes a leaf portable across harnesses; it does not make harnesses equivalent or certify their behavior. It names the checks and the vocabulary — the runtime supplies compute, and acceptance still re-runs everything independently.

deep dive S17 · plate 17 of 66 · THE ARTIFACT — A complete leaf

Nothing on this page is new — that is the point.

The anatomy act closes with one concrete object: a complete leaf in which identity, behavior, write authority, evals, stopping rules, and lifecycle travel together — a single file you can grep, diff, review, and sign.

Walk the six pins. 1 · Identity & budget: the cap carries one name, one state, one size, one retry budget — grep answers who and what. 2 · Write authority: the moat travels inside the file as touches_paths and creates_paths, and acceptance will re-measure it from the real diff. 3 · The promise: B-1 as an observable transition a stub cannot satisfy. 4 · The witness: eval_1 names what it claims — no orphan, no unexplained green. 5 · The terminal check: one Exit Check command whose green makes a candidate, never a done. 6 · The two envelopes: signed_off and accepted, both still false, writable only by the PRE and POST stamps — authorization before work, acceptance after it.

Every mechanism from the last nine plates is visible in one greppable object — zones, the effort gate, the profile, traceability, the Validation Card. That is what “a portable unit of authority” means concretely: nothing essential lives in chat history, side-channel documents, or a runner's private state. The example follows the CSV-story leaf for continuity; its structure matches the v3 spec, and it is sanitized in the spirit of the real dogfood leaf — no genuine HMAC value appears, because the digest is evidence, not decoration.

The pin cards literally point at the lines they explain — each connector joins a card to the exact line it annotates. That is the leaf's own promise about itself: every claim traceable to a line, every line claimed by a mechanism. One leaf is useful; the next act shows how a reviewed plan makes many such leaves coherent.

  • Numbered badges in the code match the pin cards; connector lines join each card to its line.
  • The two false values in the cap are the envelopes waiting for their gates — authorization before work, acceptance after.
  • The Exit Check line is the terminal witness: one command, candidate-making, never self-declared done.
  • Comment-styled lines are human-facing summaries; every machine-checked fact is a field or a heading.

deep dive S18 · plate 18 of 66 · THE PLAN — Preview before files

Rehearse the architecture before it costs a file.

Delegating a feature to coding agents usually starts by writing task files — this page explains the rehearsal that lets you argue about the shape of the work while changing it is still free.

The failure mode it kills is familiar: ask a model to “add payments reporting” and it will happily emit a pile of task files with overlapping paths and vague scopes, and once those files exist, other tooling starts referencing their IDs — cleanup becomes surgery. taskspec plan moves the argument earlier. The agent writes one TaskPlan manifest — YAML listing every proposed unit with its id, effort, depends_on, touches_paths, and creates_paths — and the CLI grades that topology without creating a single task file.

Read the five chips as the preview's report card. Units: every proposed task listed with kind and size. Edges: each depends_on must name a real unit in the same plan — nothing dangling. Sizes: every unit passes the effort gate, so nothing oversized sneaks in dressed as a leaf. Paths: all declared write surfaces laid side by side. Conflicts: two units claiming the same write path fail here, where the fix is still a one-line edit. Then the whole proposal is sealed under one digest — change any character and the hash changes.

Read the bottom token precisely. TASK_PLAN=OK means structurally reviewable, not human-authorized — the manifest still says approved: false. The preview is a verdict about shape, not about wisdom: a well-formed plan can still be the wrong plan. Judgment enters at the next gate, which is where the digest pays off — batch will bind its receipt to this hash, so a plan swapped after review is visible at materialization time.

Until then the proposal remains what the callout says: an argument, not a commitment. No files, no IDs on disk, no backlog entries — cheap to regenerate, safe to reject. The model may propose the graph; a person decides whether it becomes work.

How to read the plate
  • The YAML window is the proposal itself — what the agent wrote, before any of it is real.
  • The terminal card is the read-only validation: the unit table plus the TASK_PLAN=OK verdict, zero files written.
  • The five chips are the preview cards — units, edges, sizes, paths, conflicts — one per check that ran.
  • The two callouts split the verdict: what was checked, and what deliberately did not happen.
The boundary

A green preview proves structure, not sense — the plan can pass every check and still be a bad idea. That is deliberate: structural validation is cheap and mechanical, and the human judgment it protects gets spent at the next gate, not on hunting typos in YAML.

Approve
the barrier · plan, then batch

No approval, no task files.

Between the proposal and the filesystem stands one human decision. The model may draft the topology; only approved: true — set by a person — lets batch turn it into files. And even then, never over an existing one.

where architecture enters This gate is the one place human architectural judgment is required by the machine — everything after it can be checked; this one thing must be decided.
Story: the preview asked a question; this slide is the answer point. Walk the rail: plan proposes and writes nothing. The gold post is a person reading the topology and flipping approved: true — the refusal string under the post is the tool's real error when generation is attempted without it. Past the gate, batch fans the approved manifest into three ready files, each born with signed_off false, and emits a materialization receipt bound to the plan digest — created three, skipped zero. The red note under batch is the second protection: an existing file is never overwritten; a regenerated plan cannot silently replace what a human reviewed. Close on the footer: this is the one place the machine requires human architectural judgment — everything downstream is checkable; this is decidable only by a person. Transition: the approved graph still distinguishes organization from work — composition versus leaves is next. deep dive S19 · plate 19 of 66 · THE BARRIER — Plan, then batch

One human flag stands between the proposal and the filesystem.

Everything the planner did was reversible; generation is not — this page is about the single gate where a person authorizes a reviewed topology to become real task files.

Why a barrier at all? Once task files exist they have IDs, other files reference them, and Git starts recording history around them. So Task-Spec makes materialization impossible until a human flips one field on the exact plan they reviewed: approved: true. Attempt generation without it and the tool refuses outright — TaskPlan must set approved: true before generation. The refusal is mechanical, not advisory: the CLI checks the field and exits.

Past the gate, taskspec batch --plan is deliberately uncreative. It materializes only the declared, reviewed manifest — it never invents units to fill gaps — and it is non-clobbering: if a target file already exists, the run stops with target already exists — pick a different slug. Together with the preview's digest, that means a regenerated plan cannot silently replace what a person reviewed: the materialization receipt binds its created/skipped counts to the exact plan hash, so review and write stay auditable as one event.

Notice what each newborn file says: status: ready, signed_off: false. Approving the plan authorizes the topology — which leaves exist and how they connect. It does not seal any leaf for execution; every leaf is born unsealed and earns its own authorization later, before any attempt. Authority arrives in layers, each a separate human decision — one yes never becomes a blank check.

The footer's claim is the act's thesis: this gate is the one place the machine requires human architectural judgment. Everything downstream — sealing, handoff, acceptance — can be checked mechanically; whether the system should be built this way cannot. The plan proposes; the person disposes.

How to read the plate
  • The gold post is the human review — the rail physically stops there while approved is false.
  • The red refusal strings are the tool's real errors: no approval, no generation; existing target, no overwrite.
  • The fan-out is batch writing exactly the approved manifest — three leaf files, nothing invented.
  • The receipt binds created/skipped counts to the plan digest, so what was reviewed is what was written.
Why this page exists

Every later gate trusts that task files came from a reviewed manifest. If generation could run ahead of judgment — or quietly overwrite it afterward — the seals, closures, and receipts of the next acts would be auditing artifacts nobody chose.

Epic
the decomposition · shallow and explicit

Composition organizes. Only leaves execute.

The three files now hang under one XL parent. The parent owns children and zero write paths — it can be tracked, reported, and closed, but it can never be handed to an executor. And where a fact is missing, the plan holds a blocked hole instead of an invention.

the guard Holes stay blocked until a human supplies the fact — a plan with an honest gap beats a plan padded with guesses.
Story: the plan slide made three files; this slide shows the shape they hang in. The XL parent is a dashed frame on purpose — it is organization, not work: it owns its three children and zero write paths, so the red arrow from the parent to the executor dies at the refusal node. The green arrow shows the only legal route: one leaf at a time, through the handoff, after the PRE gate. Inside the frame, dependencies are explicit — the scheduler and the audit log both wait on the CSV export. And the fourth slot is the honest part: email delivery has an unanswered question, so it exists as a blocked hole; the planner does not manufacture a mail provider to make the plan look finished. Close on the caption: the epic is a folder with a receipt, not a unit of work. Transition: once materialized, Markdown and Git can be projected into a deterministic graph — derived, never a second source of truth. deep dive S20 · plate 20 of 66 · THE DECOMPOSITION — Shallow and explicit

An epic with no write surface can never be run.

Real work arrives as a hierarchy — epics containing tasks — and the first safety question is which nodes may execute. Task-Spec's answer is absolute: only leaves; composition nodes never do.

There are two kinds of nodes and they are not interchangeable. A composition node (XL/XXL) owns children and zero write paths — it exists so work can be tracked, reported, and closed at the level humans think about. A leaf (XS/S/M/L) owns behavior and a bounded write surface, and it is the only thing an executor may ever receive. The plate draws the rule as geometry: the arrow from the XL parent to the executor dies at a crossed node, because composition is not work.

This kills the “epic as task” failure. A task whose write surface cannot be named cannot be bounded, sealed, or verified — and a parent allowed to execute would absorb new files with no gate noticing, which is how scope silently grows. Forcing every byte of write surface onto a leaf keeps the effort gate meaningful and the hierarchy honest. Shallow and explicit is the design rule: deep nesting hides write surface.

Inside the frame, the three leaves are wired by explicit leaf-to-leaf dependency arrows — the scheduler and the audit log both wait on the CSV export. A dependency edge is ordering, not containment: it says what must finish first, never who owns whom. Containment is drawn one way, the dashed frame; dependency another, the solid luminous arrows — two relations, two pictures.

The fourth slot is the honest part. Email delivery has an unanswered question — which mail provider? — so it exists as a blocked hole: status: blocked, fact missing. The planner does not manufacture a provider to make the plan look finished; a plan with an honest gap beats a plan padded with guesses, because the gap is greppable and the guess is not.

How to read the plate
  • The dashed XL frame is a composition node: owns children, owns no paths — tracked and closed, never executed.
  • The solid cards are leaves; each names the files it may touch.
  • The luminous arrows between leaves are dependency edges — ordering only, never ownership.
  • The dashed hole card is a blocked slot: a known unknown, kept visible instead of invented away.
  • The two executor arrows are the whole rule: leaf → handoff OK; parent → never handed off.
Key detail

The handoff consumes one leaf at a time, after the PRE gate — never a composition node. That single exclusion is what stops an epic from reaching an executor with an unbounded, unverifiable scope attached.

View
the graph · taskgraphview/v1

The graph is derived — never a second source of truth.

There is no task database to drift out of sync. The task files and Git are the state; the graph is a deterministic, read-only projection of them — delete it, rerun, and you get the identical view.

no drift by construction taskspec graph --check taskspec graph --mermaid A view can be wrong only if the files are — fix the file, never the view.
Story: everything so far lives in files; this slide answers how you see the whole. Left: the three leaves and Git — the only two witnesses of state. Center: the projector — TaskGraphView is computed on demand, read-only, and deterministic: same inputs, same view, always. Right: what falls out. Structure: nodes, edges, resolved parents. Health: the three lies a plan can tell — cycles, dangling references, and two leaves claiming the same write path — all caught before any run. Scheduling: the ready frontier, dependency closure, and write-disjoint concurrency groups, which is exactly what TaskMesh will consume later. deep dive S21 · plate 21 of 66 · THE GRAPH — Derived, never authoritative

Delete the view and rerun — nothing was lost.

When the truth lives in files, you still need to see the whole system at once — without building a second truth that can drift. The answer is a graph that is computed, never stored.

The alternative is the trap: a task database. The moment state lives in two places — files plus rows — every sync bug becomes a lie about reality, and the lie surfaces at the worst moment, when something gets scheduled from stale data. Task-Spec refuses the duplication. The Markdown task files and Git are the state — the only two witnesses — and TaskGraphView/v1 is a deterministic, read-only projection of them: same inputs, same view, always. Delete the projection, rerun the command, and the identical view returns — the title's experiment is the proof.

Look at what falls out of the projector. Structure: nodes, edges, parents and children resolved. Health: the three lies a plan can tell — cycles, dangling references, and two leaves claiming the same write path — all found before anything runs. Scheduling: the ready frontier, dependency closures, and write-disjoint concurrency groups. Every answer is recomputable; none of it is a stored claim.

The two command chips are the entire interface: taskspec graph --check validates, taskspec graph --mermaid draws. There is no mutation verb because there is nothing to mutate — which is what makes the caption an invariant rather than a hope: a view can be wrong only if the files are, so fix the file, never the view.

This is the derived graph discipline the rest of the book leans on. The frontier on the next page, the concurrency waves after it, and the closure that freezes a handoff are all projections of this same graph — and the optional local control plane much later consumes exactly these answers. Canonical authority never moves off the leaves.

How to read the plate
  • The left cards are the only witnesses: the task Markdown files, plus Git as the second reader of history.
  • The cyan projector computes TaskGraphView/v1 on demand — read-only, deterministic.
  • The three right cards are what falls out: structure, health, scheduling.
  • The command chips are the whole interface — check and draw; there is no write verb.
Why this page exists

Every scheduling concept in this act is one of these projections. If the graph were a stored second source, each could drift independently; because it is derived, the worst case is deleting the view and recomputing — which is why the book says derived graph from here on.
