Ready
the frontier · eligible now

Ready means more than status: ready

Five of these six say they are ready — the frontier admits one. Eligible means a valid leaf, every dependency done, a current Tier-1 seal, and no collision. Everything else waits, with its reason spelled out.

block reasons are typed dependency unsigned / stale node-not-leaf graph invalid write conflict superseded — never just “not ready”.
Story: the scheduler-safe view, before any scheduler exists. Walk the graph: the XL parent is organization, never on the frontier. CSV export is the only node that passes all four tests — valid leaf, no waiting dependencies, a current Tier-1 seal, no collision — so it alone glows. The scheduler and audit log both say ready in their status field, but the frontier knows their dependency is not done. Report styles is the subtle one: it was gated once, then someone edited it — the seal is stale, and stale means re-gate, not trust. Email delivery still waits on its missing fact. Then the strip: taskspec ready returns exactly one line, and the caption is the point — a queue you can trust is short, and honest about why. The chip row lists every typed block reason, including two the story does not show: graph invalid and superseded. deep dive S22 · plate 22 of 66 · THE FRONTIER — Eligible now

Five say ready. The frontier admits one.

A status field is a claim a task makes about itself; the frontier is the recomputed, scheduler-safe answer to what may run right now — and it is deliberately, usefully stricter.

The gap between the two is the point of the plate: five of six nodes say status: ready, yet exactly one is eligible. Eligibility is rederived from the derived graph, not read off the file. The node must be a valid leaf — composition nodes never qualify; every dependency must be done; the sealed TaskRevision must be current at an acceptable authority tier; and no blocking collision may exist on its write surface. Anything else waits, with its reason spelled out.

Walk the failures, because they teach the rule. The scheduler and the audit log both say ready, but their dependency has not finished — blocked, dependency. Report styles is the subtle one: it passed a gate once, then someone edited it, so its seal is stale — and stale means re-gate, not trust. Email delivery still waits on its missing fact. The XL parent was never a candidate at all: node, not leaf.

Crucially, every exclusion carries a typed block reason — dependency, unsigned/stale, node-not-leaf, graph invalid, write conflict, superseded — never a shrug like “not ready.” Typed reasons make the queue actionable: a human or a pipeline can see whether the fix is finishing a dependency, re-sealing a leaf, or repairing the plan. Six nodes, six verdicts, zero ambiguity.

Note what does not exist yet: a scheduler. This is the scheduler-safe view introduced before any execution machinery, so that whatever consumes it later — a human picking work, CI, or the optional local control plane — reads the same honest answer. The terminal strip is the whole contract: taskspec ready returns exactly one line. A queue you can trust is short, and it can always say why.

How to read the plate
  • The green card is the only leaf passing every test: valid leaf, no open dependencies, current seal, no collision.
  • Red cards are blocked on dependencies; amber is a stale seal — edited after its stamp, so it must re-gate.
  • The outlined parent sits above the frontier by construction: node, not leaf.
  • The terminal strip shows taskspec ready returning exactly one line — the frontier as a command.
  • The chip row lists every typed block reason, including the two this story does not show.
Key detail

The frontier is recomputed from the derived graph on every call — never stored, so it cannot drift from the files it reads. status: ready is an input to that computation, never the verdict.

Waves
the concurrency · disjoint or contested

Parallel is a write-set decision.

CSV export is done; the scheduler and the audit log are both eligible. May they run at the same time? Not a judgment call — compare their write sets. Disjoint runs together; contested waits for the next wave.

the four relationships
disjoint write setssame wave — run together
same existing filewrite conflict — one waits
same new filedual-create error — fix the plan
dependency edgelater wave — order preserved
deterministic, not moody
Groups fall out of the declared paths — same files, same waves, every time. No scheduler opinion, nothing to tune.
why it scales Declared write surfaces make parallelism a set computation — ten agents can work one repo without stepping on each other.
Story: the frontier said what may run; this says what may run together. Wave one: the scheduler and the audit log write different files, so they flow in parallel — neither can corrupt the other, by construction. Below: schedule alerts also claims schedule.py, and its rail stops at the write-conflict node. Point at the amber continuation: contested is not refused — it is deferred to wave two, after the file is free. The panel names all four relationships, including the one the picture does not show: two leaves both creating the same new file is a dual-create error, a plan bug to fix, not to schedule around. Close on the callout: groups are computed from declared paths — same files, same waves, every time — which is what lets many agents share one repository safely, and it is exactly the grouping TaskMesh will lease from later. deep dive S23 · plate 23 of 66 · THE CONCURRENCY — Disjoint or contested

Same file, same problem — different files, same wave.

Whether two agents may work at the same time sounds like a judgment call; Task-Spec reduces it to set arithmetic over paths each leaf has already declared.

The mechanism: every leaf declares its write surface — touches_paths for existing files, creates_paths for new ones. The graph intersects those sets and builds deterministic concurrency groups containing only write-disjoint leaves. There is no scheduler opinion and nothing to tune: same files, same waves, every time. Because the inputs are declared up front, the answer is stable enough to plan a day around.

The comparison table is the entire decision procedure, four rows. Disjoint write sets land in the same wave and run together. Same existing file is a write conflict — one waits; the two leaves cannot share a wave. Same new file is a dual-create error — a plan bug to fix, not a situation to schedule around. A dependency edge simply means a later wave, with order preserved.

The plate walks two of those rows. The scheduler writes schedule.py, the audit log writes audit.py — disjoint, so both rails glow green through wave 1. Schedule alerts also claims schedule.py: its rail stops at the red write-conflict node — the annotation names the table row exactly — then continues amber as a deferral: not refused, just later, after the file is free. A contested lane is a write conflict, never a dependency ordering; the later-wave row belongs to dependency edges alone.

This is what lets many agents share one repository without corrupting each other — parallelism by construction, computed from the same derived graph the frontier came from, and the same grouping the optional local control plane leases later. One honest caveat: disjointness is a declared-path property. It rules out file collisions; it does not certify that two changes are semantically compatible — that judgment still belongs to review and to the acceptance gates.

How to read the plate
  • The green lanes are wave 1: two leaves, two different files, running in parallel.
  • The red lane claims a file already claimed — its rail stops at the write-conflict node.
  • The amber continuation is the deferral: contested means a later wave, not a refusal.
  • The table is the whole rule: four relationships, four deterministic outcomes.
  • The wave markers on the right are computed, not chosen — group membership falls out of the declared paths.
The boundary

Concurrency groups answer exactly one question — can these attempts write at the same time without corrupting each other's files. They say nothing about whether the work is good; write-disjoint is a filesystem property, and behavior is still proven at the gates.

Freeze
the closure · revision-bound context

The closure freezes what this leaf depends on.

Before the scheduler is handed off, its world is photographed: the leaf itself, every dependency it stands on, and the parents it reports to — each as an exact revision. If any of them changes later, the handoff is provably stale, not quietly wrong.

why freeze it If a dependency is re-planned mid-attempt, the digest no longer matches — the handoff is refused as CLOSURE_DRIFT instead of finishing against a world that no longer exists.
Story: last graph slide before the seal act. The spotlight metaphor: before the scheduler is handed off, photograph its world. In the light: the leaf itself, the dependency it stands on (CSV export, now done and accepted), and the composition parent it reports to — each captured as task-id plus exact TaskRevision. Outside the light, deliberately: the audit sibling and wave-2 alerts — their edits cannot stale this handoff, which keeps the freeze minimal and cheap. The three pairs flow into one sha256 — the closure digest — one hash for the whole frozen world. The payoff sentence is the footer: if anything in the light is re-planned mid-attempt, POST refuses the result as CLOSURE_DRIFT rather than accepting work built on a vanished world. Transition: and when work does change materially, the closure must not be silently rewritten — replanning creates new authority. Sources: spec/schemas/task-handoff.schema.json (closure_digest); src/graph/task_graph.py; src/dispatch/handoff.py.
deep dive S24 · plate 24 of 66 · THE CLOSURE — Revision-bound context

Photograph the world before you hand off the work.

A task is planned against a particular state of the world — finished dependencies, known parents — and if that world can change silently mid-attempt, no verdict about the attempt means much. The closure makes “the world changed” detectable.

What goes into the photograph: the leaf itself, its transitive dependencies, and its composition ancestors — each captured as a task_id plus its exact TaskRevision. Just as important is what stays out: siblings, unrelated descendants, next wave's neighbors. The freeze is minimal on purpose — cheap to compute, and precise about what can invalidate the work. The dimmed audit-log sibling can change all it wants; its edits cannot stale this handoff.

The ordered pairs are hashed into a single value: closure_digest = sha256(ordered task_id + revision pairs). One hash stands for the whole frozen world and can be rechecked in microseconds. Ordering matters: the same pairs in a different order hash differently, so the digest is canonical, not conversational. And as the plate shows, the digest travels inside the handoff packet — the check rides along with the work wherever the attempt executes.

The payoff lands later, at the gates: if anything inside the light is re-planned while the attempt is underway, the recomputed digest no longer matches, and the result is refused as CLOSURE_DRIFT — instead of accepting work that finished against a world that no longer exists. This page is what makes the stale-handoff and recovery checks of the next act possible.

Hold the boundary precisely: the digest detects change; it does not judge whether the change matters or what to do about it. A drifted closure is a refusal, not a repair — the repair is a human replan, which is exactly where the act goes next. Detection without judgment is what keeps the check fast enough to run on every handoff.

How to read the plate
  • The lit cards are the frozen world: the leaf being handed off, its done dependency, its composition parent.
  • The dimmed cards are deliberately outside the light — their changes cannot stale this handoff.
  • The three revision chips are the raw pairs: task_id plus TaskRevision, ordered.
  • The gold bar is the formula: one sha256 over the pairs.
  • The cyan chip is where the digest goes: into the TaskHandoff/v3 packet.
Why this page exists

Every later “stale” verdict — handoff checks, acceptance refusals — reads this digest. Freezing context as TaskRevision pairs turns “the plan changed underneath the worker” from a silent corruption into a typed, checkable refusal.

SOURCES · [N] spec/schemas/task-handoff.schema.json · [I] src/graph/task_graph.py, src/dispatch/handoff.py — the digest is computed from the graph, never edited by hand. If the work changes materially, the closure must not be silently rewritten. — next: the recovery.
Redo
the recovery · supersede, never mutate

Replanning creates new authority.

Mid-story, finance changes the ask: the scheduler must also honor bank holidays — a materially different job. The sealed leaf is not quietly edited; it is parked with its history, and a successor is born that must earn its own seal.

three honest moves typo before execution → amend + reseal material change → successor + supersedes interrupted → park_with_context — pick by size of the change, never by convenience.
Story: act three closes with what happens when reality changes the plan. The requirement is materially different — bank holidays change scope, not spelling. The honest path: the sealed predecessor parks with its context and partial evidence still readable; a successor is created carrying supersedes, born with signed_off false, and it must earn its own seal; the audit dependent is re-pointed and re-gated because its closure changed. The shortcut — editing the sealed file in place — fails mechanically, not morally: any authority-bearing edit changes the TaskRevision, the HMAC no longer matches, trust drops to Tier 3, and the silent downstream rewrite never happens. The chips give the full decision rule: a typo before execution may amend and reseal; a material change gets a successor; an interruption parks. Close on the caption: history stays greppable forever. Transition: the leaf is shaped — act four begins at the PRE gate, which decides whether it may run. Sources: spec/task-spec-v3.md (supersedes); docs/guides/replanning-and-recovery.md.
deep dive S25 · plate 25 of 66 · THE RECOVERY — Supersede, never mutate

History is append-only, even when the plan changes.

Halfway through the story, reality edits the requirements — this page is about recovering honestly: the sealed past is never rewritten, and new work earns new authority.

The scenario: finance changes the ask — the scheduler must also honor bank holidays. A material change, not a typo. The tempting shortcut is to edit the sealed leaf in place, and the plate shows why it fails mechanically rather than morally: any authority-bearing edit changes the TaskRevision, the HMAC v3 seal over those canonical bytes — computed under a shared key — no longer matches, and trust drops to Tier 3. The silent downstream rewrite never happens, because the gate can see it.

The honest path has three moves. The sealed predecessor parks with its context — its history and partial evidence stay readable. A successor leaf is created carrying supersedes pointing back, born signed_off: false: it inherits the work, never the trust, and must earn its own seal through a new authorization decision. And the dependents are manually re-pointed and re-gated, because their closures changed the moment their dependency was superseded.

The chips generalize the rule — pick by the size of the change, never by convenience. A typo before execution may amend and reseal; materially different or partially executed work gets a successor with supersedes; an interrupted attempt parks with context. Three moves, all auditable, none of them a rewrite. Note what is missing from the list: editing a sealed leaf and hoping nobody notices.

Why the insistence: auditability. The old leaf, its park reason, and the succession line stay greppable forever — the history card under the changed leaf is that promise drawn: revision, reason, and evidence survive side by side with the new authority. Recovery you cannot audit is just mutation with better manners. This closes the act: the leaf is shaped, and next the PRE gate decides whether it may run.

How to read the plate
  • The cyan leaf is the sealed original whose requirement changed mid-attempt.
  • The upper rail is the honest path: park the predecessor, create a successor with supersedes, re-gate it.
  • The purple history card is what survives the park: revision, reason, and partial evidence — readable forever.
  • The silver card is the dependents, re-pointed by hand and re-gated because their closure changed.
  • The red path is the forbidden shortcut: edit the sealed file and the TaskRevision seal breaks — Tier 3.
Key detail

Supersession creates new authority — the successor inherits the work, never the trust. Born signed_off: false, it re-earns its seal like any other leaf, which is what keeps a replan from laundering unreviewed scope into a running system.

the dod · is the spec provable?

deep dive S26 · plate 26 of 66 · THE DOD — Is the spec provable?

The exam paper is ready. Nobody has sat it yet.

Long before anyone asks whether the work is good, Task-Spec asks whether the question is fair — this page explains the check that grades the exam paper, not the answers.

The Definition of Done is a completeness audit of the leaf itself. The plate shows it as a matrix: behaviors on the rows — what must become true, in plain language — and evals on the columns, the commands that could prove it. A ✓ cell means this eval witnesses that behavior. The rule is simple: every row must have at least one witness, every column must name the rows it covers, and one eval must be terminal — the entire Exit Check runnable as a single command.

Now read the terminal on the right, which is where the plate earns its title. The traceability marks are checked — [x] B-1 → eval_1 — because the mapping exists. The checklist boxes are empty — [ ] eval_1, [ ] eval_2 — because nothing has run yet. And the verdict is still DOD=COMPLETE. That is not a bug: completeness is a property of the questions, not the answers. Remove one witness and the token flips to DOD=GAPS, and the seal you will meet on the next page is refused before it starts.

This distinction exists because two failures look identical from a distance: a task implemented badly, and a task that was never verifiable at all. Collapsing them is how teams end up arguing with agents about what “done” meant. DoD draws the line early, while fixing the spec is still cheap — it certifies that the task can be proven, and stays silent about whether the proof currently passes.

Keep the plate's footer as the map of the whole lifecycle: DoD certifies the exam paper, the attempt sits the exam, POST grades it — three different events, never one word. The first of those events is read-only and runs in milliseconds; the other two belong to later acts.

How to read the plate
  • Rows are behaviors — B-1, B-2, B-3 — what must become true, not what was changed.
  • Columns are evals; a ✓ says that command witnesses that row. The ★ column is terminal: the whole Exit Check as one command.
  • An off cell (—) is honest absence: that eval says nothing about that behavior.
  • The verdict has two states: DOD=COMPLETE when every row is witnessed, DOD=GAPS the moment one is not.
Why this page exists

Delegation fails quietly when “the task is well-specified” and “the work is done” share a word. By certifying the spec before any attempt exists, DoD keeps every later verdict traceable to the paper, the sitting, or the grading — never blurred into one complaint.

Gate
the pre gate · safe to delegate

PRE is a fail-closed pipeline.

Five checks stand between a well-written leaf and its seal. Any miss stops the rail with a typed refusal — the stamp is the last step of a pipeline, never a signature shortcut.

stamptaskspec gate --stamp tasks/T-20260826-export-scheduler-v2.mdexit 0
effort: S — leaf ✓ · validate: OK v3 (profile: standard) · DOD=COMPLETE evals: extracted 2 · shellcheck clean · executed — behave as declared VERDICT=DELEGATE TIER=1 signed_off: true · by luan · hmac-sha256-v3 over TaskRevision/v1
the honest edge case
A check that only proves a file exists is a weak witness — the gate lets it pass only annotated or supervised, so weak proof is visible instead of laundered into Tier 1.
fail-closed The pipeline never averages — four passes and one miss is a refusal, and the miss says its own name.
Story: the seal from the receipt-gate slide finally closes, and this shows what stands before it. Walk the five: effort — is it leaf-sized, XL and XXL are sent back to decompose. Validator — schema and profile-aware zones. DoD — the matrix from the last slide, gaps block here. Shell integrity — the evals are extracted and linted; a check that cannot parse cannot protect anyone. Then the strictest: the evals actually run, now — and red on the unpatched repo is fine, that is what discriminating means; what must not happen is an eval that crashes or lies. Only after all five does gate --stamp compute the TaskRevision and sign it: VERDICT=DELEGATE TIER=1. The callout is the honest edge: existence-only checks pass only annotated or supervised, so weak proof stays visible. Close on the footer: the pipeline never averages — one miss is a refusal that says its own name. Transition: the stamp does not sign a filename; it signs a canonical revision — TaskRevision is next. deep dive S27 · plate 27 of 66 · THE PRE GATE — Safe to delegate

Four passes and one miss is a refusal.

A human's signature should be the last thing that happens to a task, not the first — the PRE gate is the fail-closed pipeline that earns the right to sign.

Five checks stand on one rail, in a fixed order. The effort gate asks whether the task is actually a leaf — XS through L; XL and XXL are composition nodes and are sent back to decompose. The validator checks the schema and the profile-aware zones. The DoD matrix from the previous page must be complete. Shell integrity extracts the declared evals and lints them — a check that cannot parse cannot protect anyone. Finally, the strictest post: the evals are executed, now, before any stamp exists.

Fail-closed means the pipeline never averages. Four passes and one miss is a refusal, and the miss says its own name as a typed token — INVALID_TASK, DOD=GAPS, EVAL_MALFORMED, EVAL_BROKEN. You can grep a refusal; you cannot grep a shrug. Only when all five survive does gate --stamp compute the revision and sign it: VERDICT=DELEGATE TIER=1|2.

Two subtleties keep the pipeline honest. Red is allowed: on the unpatched repository a good behavioral eval should fail — that is what discriminating means, so a failing eval does not block the seal, while a broken one does. And weak proof is not laundered into strength: a check that only proves a file exists passes only annotated or supervised, so its weakness stays visible all the way to acceptance.

This is why authorization in Task-Spec is an event with evidence, not a mood. The stamp is not a signature shortcut; it is the terminal node of a pipeline that has already survived everything cheap enough to check before work begins. The order matters: the cheap structural checks run before the expensive execution check, so a malformed leaf dies fast and costs nothing.

How to read the plate
  • The posts are numbered because order is fixed — size, structure, provability, shell integrity, execution.
  • The red drip under each post is that post's typed refusal token; any one stops the rail.
  • The gold stamp node is the only exit, and it is reached last — never first.
  • The terminal card condenses the real token shapes: VERDICT=DELEGATE TIER=1, signed_off: true.
Key detail

The honest edge case is existence-only proof. A test -f check is a weak witness: PRE lets it through only annotated or supervised, so a thin eval is still visibly thin at acceptance time instead of being silently promoted to Tier-1 confidence.

sha256
the revision · canonical authority

The stamp signs a revision, not a filename.

Before signing, the leaf is reduced to what carries authority: the file is normalized, the mutable reporting envelope falls away, and what remains is hashed. Edit scope, budget, or a dependency and the digest changes; update a status and it does not.

the formula · src/security/task_revision.py
TaskRevision/v1 = sha256( contract # "TaskRevision/v1" + task_id + body_digest # sha256 of the markdown body + authority_manifest # canonical JSON of frontmatter − mutable envelope )
why default-to-sealed matters
The exclusion list is short and explicit; anything the format adds tomorrow is sealed automatically. A future authority field can never slip past the seal because someone forgot to list it.
Story: the stamp on the last slide needed a target, and a filename is not one. Walk the four stations. The file as on disk. Then the envelope falls out — and read the bin carefully: status, owner, priority, tags, tracker refs, and both stamp families. They are excluded on purpose, so a task can move through its lifecycle and be signed and accepted without those writes changing the thing that was authorized. Station three canonicalizes: sorted keys and fixed encoding, so whitespace and key order cannot forge a new revision; the body gets its own digest and the remaining frontmatter becomes the authority manifest. Station four hashes contract, id, body digest, and manifest digest into one TaskRevision — the exact bytes the HMAC signs and every later check compares. The caption is the intuition: rename, reflow, mark in-progress — same digest; change one path — new digest. The callout is the security design choice: default-to-sealed, exclusions explicit, so future fields cannot slip past. Transition: the same digest can be trusted at three very different levels — tiers next. Sources: src/security/task_revision.py (MUTABLE_FIELDS, payload); src/security/stamp.py; docs/reference/task-revision.md.
deep dive S28 · plate 28 of 66 · THE REVISION — Canonical authority

Sign the meaning, not the file.

A signature is only as strong as its target — and a filename is a terrible target, because the bytes behind it change every time someone updates a status field.

So before signing, Task-Spec reduces the leaf to exactly what carries authority, in four stations. The file enters as it sits on disk. Then the mutable envelope falls away — a short, explicit allow-list of reporting fields: status, blocked_reason, owner, priority, tags, tracker references, and the stamp fields themselves. What remains is canonicalized — sorted keys, fixed encoding, no whitespace games, so the same meaning always produces the same bytes: the markdown body gets its own digest, and the surviving frontmatter becomes the authority manifest. Finally those are hashed together: TaskRevision/v1 = sha256(contract + task_id + body_digest + authority_manifest).

The envelope exclusion is what makes the seal livable. A task must move through its lifecycle — ready to in-progress, a tracker projection written — without a human re-signing every step. Those fields report on the work; they do not authorize it, so they may change without changing the digest. The stamps live in the bin on purpose.

The opposite direction is default-to-sealed, and it is the security design choice on the page. Everything not on the short exclusion list is sealed — including fields the format has not invented yet. A future authority field can never slip past the seal because someone forgot to list it; it is sealed by default, never by exception.

The payoff is the caption under the diagram: rename the file, reflow the whitespace, mark it in-progress — same digest. Change one path in the moat — new digest. This TaskRevision is the exact byte string the HMAC signs, and the exact one every later gate recomputes and compares.

How to read the plate
  • Station 2's red bin is the only place fields may move after sealing — reporting, never authority.
  • Station 3's cyan card lists what stays sealed — note the last line: even unknown future fields.
  • Canonical JSON means key order and whitespace cannot forge a new revision.
  • The gold digest is one hash over identity, graph edges, write surface, behavior and evals, budgets, and execution policy.
Key detail

Default-to-sealed inverts the usual failure mode. Systems that list what to protect forget things; Task-Spec lists what may move — a list short enough to audit — and seals everything else, so tomorrow's authority field is protected on the day it is invented.

Tier
the trust tier · do not flatten the verdict

Same digest. Three levels of trust.

A seal is not a yes/no. The gate reports how much it could verify — and each tier carries its own operating policy, so a weaker proof can still be useful without pretending to be strong.

1
tier one · crypto trust
HMAC v3 verified over the current revision
The signature checks out against the repository key, and the TaskRevision it signs is the one on disk right now. Nothing authority-bearing changed since the human stamped it.
key presentsignature validrevision current
operating policyeligible for unsupervised dispatch— only if every other gate also passes
2
tier two · structural trust
Valid shape, weaker proof
The leaf is structurally sound but the seal cannot be fully verified here: the key is unavailable, the envelope is a legacy version, or the evidence is narrower than Tier 1 demands.
no key on this machinelegacy envelopenarrower proof
operating policysupervised only— a named human overrides explicitly at acceptance
3
tier three · no trust
The seal is broken or lying
The envelope is malformed, it was signed with the wrong key, or the revision on disk no longer matches what was signed — someone edited authority after the stamp.
malformedwrong keyrevision mismatch
operating policyhard refusal— no override, no supervision path, re-gate from scratch
what HMAC is not A shared-key seal is tamper evidence — it is not author identity, not sandboxing, and not proof that the eval is semantically wise.
Story: the digest from the last slide can be trusted at three levels, and the whole point is not to flatten them into a boolean. Tier one: the HMAC verifies against the repository key and the revision it signed is the one on disk — nothing authority-bearing moved — so unsupervised dispatch becomes possible, provided every other gate also passes. Tier two: structurally valid but the proof is weaker here — no key on this machine, a legacy envelope, narrower evidence — so it runs supervised only, and a named human must override explicitly at acceptance; the weakness is visible, not laundered. Tier three: malformed, wrong key, or revision mismatch — the edit-after-stamp case from the replanning slide — hard refusal with no override path. Close with the footer, which is the honesty line the deck keeps returning to: HMAC is shared-key tamper evidence, not identity, not isolation, not semantic truth. Transition: watch what a Tier-1 seal actually catches — the tamper matrix. Sources: docs/concepts/signed-off.md; src/security/stamp.py; src/gate/safe-to-delegate.sh (TIER=1|2|3 policy comments); tests/test-hmac-envelope.sh.
deep dive S29 · plate 29 of 66 · THE TRUST TIER — Do not flatten the verdict

A seal is a dial with three detents.

When the gate inspects a seal, it does not answer “valid or not” — it answers “how much could I verify, here, right now?”, and each answer carries a different way you are allowed to operate.

Tier 1 is full verification: the HMAC v3 envelope checks out against the repository key, and the TaskRevision it signs is the one on disk right now — nothing authority-bearing has moved since the human stamped it. A Tier-1 leaf is eligible for unsupervised dispatch, with a deliberate caveat: only if every other gate also passes. The tier describes the seal, not the whole world.

Tier 2 is structural trust with weaker proof: the leaf is well-formed, but this machine lacks the key, or the envelope is a legacy version, or the evidence is narrower than Tier 1 demands. The policy is supervised only, and a named human must override explicitly at acceptance. The common case is a laptop without the repository key: same leaf, same seal, but proof that cannot be fully checked here — so it runs supervised, and the record says so. The weakness is carried on the label instead of being laundered into a yes.

Tier 3 is a seal that is broken or lying: malformed envelope, wrong key, or a revision that no longer matches what was signed — someone edited authority after the stamp. The policy is a hard refusal: no override, no supervision path; the task goes back through the gate from scratch.

The footer's honesty line matters as much as the cards. An HMAC is shared-key tamper evidence — it is not author identity, not sandboxing or isolation, and not proof that the eval is semantically wise. Keep that boundary and the tiers stay useful; cross it and a seal becomes a superstition.

How to read the plate
  • The cards descend green, amber, red — the glow marks the only tier eligible for unsupervised dispatch.
  • The chips on each card are the concrete, machine-checkable conditions that produced the tier.
  • The operating-policy strip is the point: each tier says what you may do, not just what was found.
  • Tier 2's override lives at acceptance — after the work — never as a dispatch-time shortcut.
Why this page exists

Flattening the verdict into valid/invalid forces a bad choice: refuse weak-but-honest proof, or treat it as strong. Three tiers keep the middle usable — supervised, visible, and explicitly overridden by a named human at acceptance — without pretending it is Tier 1.

Tamper
the tamper matrix · what requires re-authorization

Change authority, break the seal. Report progress, keep it.

Six edits to the sealed scheduler leaf. The seal argues with nobody — it simply stops matching when an authority-bearing field moves, and stays valid when only the reporting envelope does.

operational intuition If your edit would change what the executor may do, expect to re-gate. If it only changes what the board shows, carry on.
Story: turn the cryptography into muscle memory. Read the diffs, not the labels. Widening the moat, changing a dependency, raising the budget, swapping the executor — each changes what the executor may do, so each changes the TaskRevision, the HMAC stops matching, trust drops to Tier 3, and a human must decide again. The bottom group: status moves and tracker projections are in the mutable envelope from the revision slide, so the digest is untouched and Tier 1 holds — a task can flow through its whole lifecycle without anyone re-signing it. The footer is the one-line rule to take home: would the edit change what the executor may do? then re-gate; does it only change what the board shows? carry on. Transition: once sealed, the contract is packaged as one portable attempt — the handoff. Sources: tests/test-hmac-envelope.sh; src/security/task_revision.py (MUTABLE_FIELDS).
deep dive S30 · plate 30 of 66 · THE TAMPER MATRIX — What requires re-authorization

The seal doesn't argue. It stops matching.

Once a leaf is sealed, every edit falls into one of two classes — and the difference between them is the difference between routine bookkeeping and a new task wearing an old seal.

The mechanism is pure revision logic from two pages back: the TaskRevision covers the authority-bearing fields, and the HMAC signs that digest. Edit an authority field and the digest changes, the signature no longer matches, and verification drops to Tier 3 — re-authorize. Nothing about the edit's intent matters; only the bytes do. The seal does not argue; it simply stops matching. That split is designed, not accidental: the format deliberately parks lifecycle bookkeeping in the reporting envelope, so that ordinary progress — picking the task up, noting it on a board — never invalidates the authority the work runs under. Only edits that redraw the granted power should wake the human, and those are exactly the fields the digest seals.

Read the four red diffs on the left as “what the executor may do.” Widening touches_paths enlarges the write surface. Changing depends_on changes the graph the task stands on. Raising budget_iterations extends the leash. Swapping execution_backend changes who holds the tools. Each redrew the authority the human actually granted — so each requires the human again.

The two green diffs on the right only change what the board shows. Moving status from ready to in-progress and writing a tracker_ref projection live in the mutable envelope, so the digest is untouched and the seal remains valid. A task can flow through its entire lifecycle — picked up, worked, tracked — without anyone re-signing it.

The footer is the one-line rule to internalize: would the edit change what the executor may do? Expect to re-gate. Does it only change what the board shows? Carry on. That is the tamper matrix as muscle memory — no cryptography required at the moment of the edit.

How to read the plate
  • Red diffs strike from the left and die at crossed nodes on the seal's border — authority edits never reach the leaf.
  • Green diffs pass through check nodes from the right — reporting edits land; the seal holds.
  • The center card is the sealed leaf: lock, TaskRevision digest, and the hmac-sha256-v3 envelope.
  • The verdicts are deterministic: mismatch → Tier 3; envelope-only → Tier 1 holds.
Why this page exists

Cryptographic language — integrity, authenticity — does not tell an operator what to do when someone asks to bump a budget at 17:00. This matrix turns the seal into operational intuition: authority mutation and lifecycle reporting are different classes, and only one of them wakes the human.

Packet
the handoff · one authorized attempt

TaskHandoff/v3 is the pickup packet.

Once sealed, the leaf is packaged as one attempt: which revision, on which commit, inside which frozen world, allowed to touch what, for how long, and how to come home. Every executor receives exactly this — and nothing more.

Story: the seal is closed; now the leaf becomes a packet any harness can pick up. Walk the eight pins in order, and notice most of them are things the audience already met: the TaskRevision from the revision slide, the tier from the tiers slide, the closure digest from the closure slide, the moat and do-not-touch from the contract act. New here: the attempt id — evidence produced later must name this attempt, not another — and the immutable base commit that history can be replayed from. Pin eight is the quiet one: the eval and acceptance commands ride inside, so the route back to POST is part of the job, not folklore. Then the red strip: what is never inside — the signing key, the evaluator key, holdout commands, provider credentials. The executor gets authority to act, never authority to approve. Transition: that stable packet is why the executor can change without changing the job. deep dive S31 · plate 31 of 66 · THE HANDOFF — One authorized attempt

Eight pins, one packet, no secrets.

A sealed task is never explained to an executor in prose — it is packaged, once, into a JSON packet that pins down the revision, the world, the leash, and the route home.

Read the eight pins as eight answers. Which revision — the task_revision_digest, the exact sealed bytes, not a filename or “latest.” Who authorized, at what tier — a reference to the seal, never the key itself. Which attempt — one id, and all later evidence must name this attempt, not another. On which commit — an immutable base, so history can be replayed from here. Inside which frozen world — the dependency-closure digest, so drift in the task's neighborhood is detectable.

Then the leash. Allowed to touch what — the write surface plus do-not-touch, which POST will measure again rather than trust. For how long, on what — the iteration budget and backend travel with the work, so the stop rules are part of the job, not the environment's mood. And how to come home — the eval and acceptance commands ride inside the packet, so the route back to the independent gate is part of the job definition, not folklore in a wiki.

Every executor receives exactly this packet and nothing more — same revision, same base, same closure, same scope, same budget, same acceptance route. That uniformity is what makes the next page's claim possible: the executor can change without the job changing. If any field were missing, every harness would improvise its own interpretation of the task — and portability would be a slogan instead of a schema.

The red strip is the boundary that keeps the packet safe to carry: no signing key, no evaluator key, no private holdout command, no provider credential ever enters it. The executor receives authority to act — never authority to accept its own work.

How to read the plate
  • Pins 1–3 identify the job: which revision, whose seal at what tier, which attempt id.
  • Pins 4–5 freeze the world: immutable base commit plus the closure digest from the graph act.
  • Pins 6–7 are the leash: write surface with do-not-touch, budget and backend.
  • Pin 8 is the quiet one — the route to POST ships inside the packet.
The boundary

A handoff that carried the signing key would let the worker mint its own authorization; one that carried the evaluator key would let it grade itself. The packet deliberately contains neither — authority to act travels; authority to judge stays home.

Any
the portability · harness is not authority

Same contract, different harness.

The packet does not care who picks it up. Codex, Claude Code, Kimi, Grok Build, Cursor — each runs the same leaf, same evals, same budget, and each returns to the same independent gate. Swap the tool; the job, the proof, and the verdict do not move.

what the skill is, and is not The installed skill helps each harness find and drive the CLI — it never replaces a gate, and nobody claims the models behave identically. Only the contract and the verdict are identical.
Story: this is why the packet slide mattered. One TaskHandoff fans out to five very different executors — and every rail is the same purple because the packet is the same bytes. Each harness has the skill installed, which only teaches it to find and drive the CLI; the skill is a convenience, not an authority. All five rails reconverge on one POST post that does not know, and does not need to know, which harness ran — it reruns the evals against the attempt id, and emits one receipt of one shape. Be honest on the footer: nobody claims Codex and Kimi behave identically; the claim is narrower and stronger — the contract, the proof, and the verdict are identical. Transition: portability has levels; parsing a leaf is not the same as completing its lifecycle — conformance is next. Sources: install.sh; SKILL.md; harness/; README.md; docs/guides/multi-harness.md.
deep dive S32 · plate 32 of 66 · THE PORTABILITY — Harness is not authority

The gate doesn't know which harness ran.

Portability is usually a vague promise about “working everywhere”; here it is a picture of one packet, five executors, and one gate that cannot tell them apart.

The fan-out is the claim. One TaskHandoff/v3 packet travels along five identical purple rails — identical because the bytes are identical — to Codex, Claude Code, Kimi, Grok Build, and Cursor. Each harness runs the same leaf, same evals, same budget. Nothing about the job is re-negotiated per tool, because nothing about the job lives in the tool.

What differs per harness is small and honestly labeled: the installed skill teaches each executor how to find and drive the Task-Spec CLI — where the packet is, which commands to run, how to report states. The skill is a driving lesson, not a new engine: it never replaces a gate, never widens a scope, never signs anything. The installer drops the same small skill into each harness's skill directory, so the adapter is one file per tool — not a fork of the tool, and not a second source of truth.

The reconvergence is what makes the fan-out meaningful. All five cyan rails return to one POST gate that does not know — and does not need to know — which harness ran. It reruns the evals against the attempt id and emits one AcceptanceRecord/v1 of one shape, bound to that attempt. Whoever did the work, the receipt is the same object — which is why results can be compared across runs and across tools without translation.

Hold the claim at its true size: nobody promises that Codex and Kimi behave identically — models differ, and this book never says otherwise. What is identical is the contract, the proof, and the verdict. Portability of the job, not uniformity of the worker — and for delegation, the job is the part that must not move.

How to read the plate
  • Purple rails fan out because the packet bytes are the same for every harness.
  • Each card's “skill on” line is the adapter — it finds and drives the CLI, nothing more.
  • Cyan rails reconverge: all evidence funnels into a single gate post.
  • The gold receipt is one shape, bound to the attempt — the gate is harness-blind by construction.
Why this page exists

Authority must live somewhere, and this page says where it does not: in the harness. If the tool were the authority, swapping tools would mean re-trusting the work. Because authority lives in the sealed contract and acceptance lives in the independent gate, the executor in the middle is replaceable.

L1 adds the lifecycle: claim the lock by moving to in-progress before touching anything and leave a truthful terminal status, which is what makes a shared backlog safe from double-picking. L2 adds the budget: on an unsolvable spec, stop and park with a reason instead of burning iterations — the observable test is literally an unsolvable reference spec that ends parked without timing out — and that is the bar for unattended cranking. The command certifies any executor and prints CONFORMANCE=L2; the eight chips are the real bundled suite: status lock, emit enum, no signed-off modification, execution backend, budget stop, do-not-touch, node refusal, v4 policy. deep dive S33 · plate 33 of 66 · THE EXECUTOR CONTRACT — L0 to L2

Three rungs between parsing a file and running unattended.

“Supports Task-Spec” is a meaningless claim until you say how much of the contract the executor honors — L0, L1, and L2 turn that into three rungs you can test from the outside.

L0 — read and run. Given a signed spec, the executor understands the format and produces work that makes the Exit Check return 0. A plain bash loop can reach this rung, which is exactly the point: the floor is low, and it unlocks supervised, one-shot dispatch.

L1 — honor the lifecycle. The executor claims the lock by moving the task to in-progress before touching anything, emits machine-readable states as it works, and leaves a truthful terminal status on exit. That is what makes a shared backlog safe: two executors can never double-pick one leaf. It unlocks working from a queue instead of a single hand-off.

L2 — honor the budget. On a spec it cannot satisfy within budget_iterations, the executor stops and parks with a reason instead of looping forever. The observable test is beautifully concrete: an unsolvable reference spec must end parked, not timed out. Knowing when to stop is what unlocks unattended operation.

The staircase shape is the semantics: each level adds obligations — pickup, then execution discipline, then verifiable evidence for independent acceptance — so L2 literally contains L1 and L0. taskspec conformance --level L2 --executor "my-runner --flags" runs the bundled reference behaviors against any command line and prints CONFORMANCE=L2. One nuance worth keeping: even at L2, the executor still never writes done — the accept stamp does; conformance only exercises the lifecycle transitions an executor is allowed to make. And the footer keeps the claim honest: conformance of the bundled reference path proves an adapter works — it is not an ecosystem-wide certification of everything that claims the name.

How to read the plate
  • Each taller card contains the lower obligations — the “+ honor” labels are literal.
  • The “unlocks” strip is the payoff: each rung buys a wider way of working.
  • The eight chips are the real bundled suite — status-lock through v4-policy.
  • The L2 test is behavioral: an unsolvable spec must end parked, never timed out.
The boundary

A conformance stamp travels well, so the page fences it: the bundled suite certifies the executor you point it at, on the machine where it ran. Publishing CONFORMANCE=L2 is your adapter's contract with the format — not a blanket endorsement of every executor in the ecosystem.

Loop
the runner · closed-loop proof

Evals run at agent cadence.

Inside one attempt the executor gets a fast, deterministic feedback loop: change, run the declared evals, read the verdict, go again — bounded by two counters it cannot reset. Green here makes a candidate; it never makes a done.

## Success Criteria · one behavioral eval + the terminal check
# eval_1 (verifies B-2): bank holidays are skipped python -m reports.schedule --date 2026-12-25 --dry-run \ | grep -q "SKIPPED: bank holiday" # fails on the unpatched repo # eval_2 · terminal — the whole Exit Check as one command pytest -q tests/test_schedule.py && python -m reports.verify_columns
the weak witness

the boundary of green A passing attempt is a candidate result. POST — not the runner, not the executor — decides whether it can close.
Story: this is the execution loop, and the trick is to introduce it without letting green become acceptance. Walk the ring clockwise: change the code inside the write surface; run the declared evals with taskspec run; read a verdict that names the eval and the reason; on fail, retry with reason and go around again. Two brakes sit in the center and the executor cannot reset them — the iteration budget and the no-progress breaker from the guardrails slide. Two exits leave the ring: EVAL=PASS produces a candidate that goes to POST; a tripped breaker parks with context, keeping the evidence. Right side: what a good eval looks like — a behavioral probe that fails on the unpatched repo and passes on the patch, plus the terminal Exit Check as one command. The callout names the weak witness: a file-exists check proves nothing about behavior. Footer: a passing attempt is a candidate; POST decides. deep dive S34 · plate 34 of 66 · THE RUNNER — Closed-loop proof

Two brakes the executor cannot reset.

Inside a single attempt, the executor gets a fast, deterministic feedback loop — change, evaluate, read, retry — and two brakes it cannot reset, so “trying things” can never become “running forever.”

Walk the ring clockwise. The executor changes the code, strictly inside the write surface. It runs the declared evals — the same commands the leaf sealed — via taskspec run --ci. It reads the verdict: pass, fail, which eval, and why. On failure it goes around again with retry_with_reason — the reason matters, because a loop that cannot say what it is fixing is just spinning.

The two counters in the center are the brakes, and the executor cannot reset them: the iteration budget counts attempts, and the no-progress breaker counts loops that changed nothing. Trip either one and the attempt leaves the ring as parked_with_context — stop, keep the evidence, hand the situation back to a human with the story intact.

The other exit is green: EVAL=PASS produces a candidate result, and the page insists on that word. Green inside the loop is a fact about the runner; acceptance is a decision made later, by POST, which reruns everything independently. The runner's green is an input to that decision — it is never the decision. This is the same boundary the handoff packet drew one act earlier: the worker may run the checks, but it cannot accept itself.

The code window shows what a strong eval looks like: a behavioral probe that fails on the unpatched baseline and passes on the patch — that difference is the whole value of green. Beside it sits the weak witness: test -f tests/test_schedule.py proves only that a file exists. Existence-only checks pass PRE only annotated or supervised; behavioral probes are what let a loop mean something.

How to read the plate
  • Four stations on the ring; the gold retry card is the only way around again.
  • The center counters are brakes the executor cannot reset — iterations and no-progress.
  • Two exits only: green to POST as a candidate, red to parked_with_context with evidence kept.
  • eval_1 is behavioral — it must fail on the baseline; eval_2 is the terminal Exit Check as one command.
Key detail

A loop is only as good as its probe. If the eval cannot distinguish broken from fixed, green certifies nothing — which is why discriminating power, red on the baseline and green on the patch, is a property the gate checks before the attempt, not a hope during it.

deep dive S35 · plate 35 of 66 · THE BOUNDARY — Core vs runtime

Verdicts on the left. Engines on the right. Two rails between.

Task-Spec deliberately does less than an agent platform: it produces authority and acceptance contracts, and leaves models, credentials, and sandboxes to the runtimes that already own them.

The left plate is the core: the contract and the derived graph, PRE authorization, the handoff, eval and POST acceptance, and receipts with trust policy. Its one-line caption is the discipline — it produces verdicts; it never executes. There is no model call, no credential, and no sandbox inside it, by design.

The right plate is the runtime: the model process, provider credentials, sandbox enforcement, compute and network, and actual external observation. Its caption mirrors the first — it executes inside declared limits; it never accepts its own work. Runtimes are good at exactly the things the core refuses to do, and the split keeps both auditable.

Only two things cross the boundary, one in each direction. TaskHandoff/v3 carries a single authorized attempt outward — revision, closure, moat, budget, route. AcceptanceRecord/v1 brings the evidence back — attempt-bound, independently produced, with typed refusals. Everything else is refused where it stands: credentials never enter packets, and verdicts never emerge from runtimes. Notice what that excludes in both directions — the core never learns which cloud ran the attempt, and the runtime never learns what the gate concluded beyond the evidence it produced.

This narrowness is what lets the system grow without blurring. v4 environment evidence and the optional TaskMesh local control plane attach at these two rails instead of dissolving into the core. And it sets up the next act: the boundary closes only when POST independently reconstructs what happened — acceptance is a reconstruction, not a report. If a proposed feature ever needs the core to execute, or the runtime to judge, this page says the feature is misfiled before it says anything else.

How to read the plate
  • Gold plate, left: everything that decides — authorization in, acceptance out.
  • Purple plate, right: everything that runs — models, credentials, isolation, observation.
  • The top rail is the only way out; the bottom rail is the only way back.
  • The center node on each rail is a boundary post — the only legal crossings.
Why this page exists

Every scope question in the system is answered here. Hosted execution? Outside. Credential handling? Outside. Self-acceptance? Nowhere. The book can make strong claims about verdicts precisely because the core makes none about sandboxes.

Story: the attempt came home green, and this slide is why that is not enough. Walk the rail left to right: A reruns the Exit Check — the declared evals execute again against this attempt, not against the worker's testimony. B re-measures the handoff, the base commit, the closure digest, and the blast radius; C re-checks authorization integrity against the sealed TaskRevision; D is the optional gold sanity; E applies the evidence policy before any verdict is written. deep dive S36 · plate 36 of 66 · THE POST GATE — Independent acceptance

The second green is the one that counts.

A worker finishing green only ever produces a candidate — this page explains the independent gate that turns a candidate into an accepted attempt, or refuses it by name.

Everything before this act authorized the work and watched it run; POST is the moment the system decides what may close. The acceptor is independent of the executor, so it trusts nothing the attempt says about itself. Rather than replaying the worker's log, it re-derives the verdict from the artifacts — the runner's green made a candidate, and it never made a done.

Read the rail as five checks in a fixed order. A reruns the Exit Check — the declared evals execute again, against this attempt, not against the worker's report of them. B re-measures the world: the handoff packet, the base commit, the frozen closure, and the blast radius are measured, not remembered. C checks authorization integrity — the TaskRevision digest must still equal the sealed bytes, so a mutated contract is a refusal, not a diff. D is the optional gold sanity, and E applies the evidence policy: external receipts count only under the trust the leaf configured.

Only when all five hold does the rail reach its terminal node — AcceptanceRecord/v1, one durable object bound to this attempt. Any miss stops the rail with a typed refusal: EVAL_FAILED, POLICY_TAMPER, HANDOFF_STALE, CLOSURE_DRIFT, BLAST_RADIUS, or BASE_DIVERGED — grep-able tokens, never prose, so pipelines and humans can branch on exactly what failed.

Hold the distinction the title draws. A replay button reproduces the worker's run; a second gate re-derives it. Authorization happened before the work; acceptance happens after it — and acceptance, alone, writes the record the lifecycle will later call done. That is why the gate reruns proof instead of trusting testimony: the verdict has to survive contact with someone who was not rooting for it.

How to read the plate
  • The five gold cards A–E are the checks, in order — each a gate the attempt must pass, not a step the worker reports.
  • The luminous rail runs left to right because order matters: evidence policy is applied before any verdict is written.
  • The green terminal node is not a sixth check — it is the object the checks earn: AcceptanceRecord/v1.
  • The red chips are typed refusals; any one stops the rail and names why.
Why this page exists

The act opens here because every mechanism that follows — blast radius, gold sanity, receipts — is one stop on this rail. If you can retell A through E, you can place every page that comes after.

Diff
the diff · committed + staged + unstaged + untracked

Blast radius reads the whole Git reality.

“The diff looked fine” only describes one layer. POST unions committed, staged, unstaged, and untracked changes into one observed-path set, then takes the set difference against the sealed write surface — so a clean-looking patch view cannot hide out-of-scope changes. One escaped path refuses the whole attempt.

hardening that makes the set honest
Realpath and symlink protections unfold aliases before the comparison, the base commit must remain an ancestor of the attempt head, and nested workspaces resolve to one canonical root — three ways a scope check is fooled, closed.
stronger than “git diff looked fine” Scope can be perfect while the eval is still meaningless — the next gate asks whether green can tell anything at all.
Story: “the diff looked fine” only ever describes one layer of the repository. Walk the left column: committed, staged, unstaged, untracked — four places a change can hide, and a patch view shows at most one of them. The four rails union into one observed-path set, and only that set is compared against the sealed write surface from the contract act. Two exits: every path inside and POST continues; one escape — a .env, a file under src/billing/ — and the whole attempt refuses BLAST_RADIUS, even if the visible patch was beautiful. The callout is the hardening that makes the set honest: realpath and symlink resolution before comparison, the base commit must remain an ancestor of the attempt head, and nested workspaces resolve to one canonical root — implemented in src/accept/preflight.py and src/lib/workspace.py, exercised by tests/test-v381-workspace.sh and tests/test-v38-hardening.sh. Keep the qualifier: this proves scope, not goodness. Transition: scope can be perfect while the eval is still meaningless.
deep dive S37 · plate 37 of 66 · THE DIFF — The whole Git reality

Four layers can hide a change. The union sees them all.

When a reviewer says “the diff looked fine,” they have opened one layer of the repository — this page explains why acceptance unions all four before it believes anything.

Git keeps changes in four places at once: committed work on the attempt branch, staged work sitting in the index, unstaged edits in the working tree, and untracked files that were never added anywhere. A patch view — the thing git diff prints — shows at most one of those layers. A worker who wants a change to escape review does not need to hide it well; it only needs to live in a layer nobody opened, like an untracked .env or a stray edit under src/billing/.

The blast-radius check therefore builds one observed-path set: the union of all four layers, resolved against a single canonical workspace root. Only that union is compared — by set difference — against the sealed write surface, the touches_paths and creates_paths the contract named before work began. Any observed path that is not in the sealed surface is an escape, and one escape refuses the whole attempt with BLAST_RADIUS, no matter how clean the visible patch was.

The plate's callout is the hardening that keeps the set honest. Realpath and symlink protections unfold aliases before comparison, so a symbolic link cannot smuggle a path past the check. The base commit must remain an ancestor of the attempt head, so history cannot be quietly re-rooted under the work. And nested workspaces resolve to one canonical root, so a repository inside a repository cannot split the measurement in two.

Hold the qualifier: this gate proves scope, not goodness. An attempt can fit its write surface perfectly while the behavior itself is still wrong — deciding whether the green means anything is the next gate's job.

How to read the plate
  • The four layer cards are where a change can live — committed, staged, unstaged, untracked — and a patch view shows at most one.
  • The glowing union node is the only thing POST actually checks: every change Git can see, under one canonical root.
  • The gold comparison gate takes the set difference against the sealed write surface — nothing else counts.
  • The green exit continues POST when every path is inside; the red dashed exit is one escaped path refusing the whole attempt.
Why this page exists

It demonstrates why acceptance is stronger than “git diff looked fine”: the check runs against the whole Git reality, not against the summary a worker chooses to show.

Green
the goodhart guard · does green mean change?

The same eval must fail, then pass.

A green run proves nothing if the eval was green before the work began. Gold sanity runs the declared evals twice: once against the unpatched baseline, where they must fail, and once against the candidate, where they must pass. Only the difference between those two runs says the patch changed the world.

gold sanity · BASELINE run — the unpatched tree
# the same evals, against the world without the patch taskspec accept --handoff a1.json --gold-sanity # eval_1 (verifies B-2): bank holidays are skipped python -m reports.schedule --date 2026-12-25 --dry-run ✗ FAIL — no SKIPPED line emitted # expected here # eval_2 · terminal check pytest -q tests/test_schedule.py ✗ FAIL — 2 failing, 11 passing BASELINE=RED ✓ the eval can see the gap
gold sanity · the verdict
the eval discriminates
red where the world lacks the behavior, green where the patch provides it — that difference is the whole value of green
gold sanity · PATCH run — attempt 7c9e
# the identical evals, against the candidate # eval_1 (verifies B-2): bank holidays are skipped python -m reports.schedule --date 2026-12-25 --dry-run ✓ PASS — “SKIPPED: bank holiday” emitted # eval_2 · terminal check pytest -q tests/test_schedule.py ✓ PASS — 13 passing PATCH=GREEN ✓ verdict: the eval discriminates
the honest qualifier
--gold-sanity is opt-in. It raises confidence that this eval discriminates on this leaf — it does not create universal semantic truth about the patch, and it never claims to.
when the baseline also passes EVAL_NONDISCRIMINATING — green that costs nothing is refused. When every gate passes, acceptance becomes a durable object.
Story: this is the Goodhart guard — the moment a metric becomes a target, green stops meaning change. Walk the two terminals: on the left the declared evals run against the unpatched baseline and must come back red; on the right the identical evals run against the candidate and must come back green. The verdict card in the middle is the difference between them — the eval discriminates, so green on this leaf actually cost something. Then the red strip: if the baseline also passes, acceptance refuses EVAL_NONDISCRIMINATING, because a test that cannot fail cannot witness anything. Land the qualifier exactly as written on the slide: --gold-sanity is opt-in, it raises confidence, and it does not create universal semantic truth — it says this eval discriminates on this leaf, nothing more. Sources: src/accept/accept-task.sh and docs/runbooks/dispatching-a-task-spec.md. Transition: when every gate passes, acceptance becomes a durable object.
deep dive S38 · plate 38 of 66 · THE GOODHART GUARD — Does green mean change?

Green is only evidence if red was possible.

A test that passes no matter what proves nothing — this page explains the opt-in check that makes an eval earn its green.

The previous gate proved the patch stayed inside its scope; it said nothing about whether the eval means anything. This is Goodhart's law applied to acceptance: the moment a green run becomes the target, it stops measuring the work. An eval can be green because the patch works — or because the eval cannot fail at all, asserting something that was already true before the attempt began. Green from such an eval costs nothing, and free green is exactly what a lazy or corner-cutting worker would love to present.

Gold sanity is the guard. With --gold-sanity, the acceptor executes the declared evals twice. First against the unpatched baseline — the world without the patch — where they must fail, because the behavior they assert does not exist yet. Then against the candidate, where they must pass. Only the difference between those two runs says the patch changed the world: red where the behavior is missing, green where the patch provides it. That difference is the entire value of green.

The failure mode gets its own typed refusal. If the baseline also passes, the eval cannot tell the world before from the world after, and acceptance stops with EVAL_NONDISCRIMINATING. The reasoning is strict: a test that cannot fail cannot witness anything, so its green carries no information about this attempt.

Keep the honest qualifier exactly as the deck states it: gold sanity is opt-in, and it raises confidence that this eval discriminates on this leaf. It does not create universal semantic truth about the patch — it never claims the behavior is correct, only that the eval can tell its absence from its presence.

How to read the plate
  • The left terminal runs the declared evals against the unpatched baseline — red is the expected, required outcome.
  • The right terminal runs the identical evals against the candidate — green is required here.
  • The gold verdict card is the difference between the two runs: the eval discriminates.
  • The red strip names the refusal when the baseline passes too — green that costs nothing is refused.
The boundary

Opt-in, and scoped: the claim is “this eval discriminates on this leaf.” Nothing here asserts universal semantic truth about the patch — the deck refuses that claim everywhere.

AcceptanceRecord/v1 is the durable verdict.

A passed gate becomes an object you can audit. Finalize writes the attempt record, the task acceptance envelope, and the metrics projection atomically — exact retries are idempotent, conflicting retries refuse. Seven fields are recorded together, so the verdict can never drift from the attempt it judged.

Walk the seven pins in order and notice the pattern — each field answers one audit question: which task, which sealed revision, which authorization, which attempt, who accepted, when, and the record's own digest. Pin four is the one the next act leans on: the attempt id, because external evidence must name this attempt, not another. deep dive S39 · plate 39 of 66 · THE RECEIPT — Attempt-bound acceptance

Seven fields, one digest, zero drift.

A passed gate is an event; what an audit needs is an object — this page explains the seven-field record that keeps a verdict attached to the exact attempt it judged.

Once every POST check holds, acceptance does not merely say yes — it writes. The AcceptanceRecord/v1 is the durable verdict, and its design goal is that the verdict can never drift from the attempt. Seven fields are recorded together: task_id (which leaf), task_revision (which sealed revision of the contract), authorization_ref (which authorization — a reference to the seal, never the key), attempt_id (which execution), accepted_by (an acceptor independent of the executor), accepted_at (when), and record_digest (the receipt's own digest).

Notice what the binding forbids. Because revision, authorization, and attempt ride in the same object, a record cannot be silently re-pointed at a different revision or a different run: change any field and the record digest stops matching. The verdict is durable precisely because it is bound — tampering with the record is detectable, and re-reading it always answers the same seven audit questions. Pin four deserves a second look: the attempt_id is the field the rest of this act leans on, because every piece of external evidence must name this attempt — not another run, not last week's.

The write semantics matter as much as the fields. Finalize writes the attempt record, the task acceptance envelope, and the metrics projection atomically — all three or none, so a crash cannot leave half a verdict on disk. Exact retries are idempotent: re-running the same acceptance rewrites the same record. Conflicting retries — the same attempt, a different verdict — refuse. A rerun never forks what “accepted” means.

Terminology, kept straight: authorization happened before the work; this record is acceptance, after it. And it is the only object the backlog lifecycle accepts as a ticket into done — which is the next page's map.

How to read the plate
  • The JSON window is the record as finalize writes it, digests redacted for display.
  • Pins 2–3 in gold point at sealed authority — the revision and the authorization reference.
  • Pin 4 in purple is the attempt id — the field external evidence will have to name.
  • Pin 5 is the independent acceptor — never the worker's self-report; pin 7 in green is the record's own digest.
Key detail

Atomic write, idempotent exact retries, refusing conflicting retries — together these mean the verdict cannot fork, even under crashes and reruns.

Done
the lifecycle · ready to done

Done is a settled state, not a worker emotion.

Backlog state moves on evidence, not enthusiasm. status: done requires accepted: true — the only two edges into done both demand an accepted receipt — and status: sealed is not a lifecycle state at all: sealing is authorization metadata, and it never appears on this map. Blocked and parked are honest branches; they return to ready, never to done.

Story: done is a settled state, not a worker emotion. Walk the common route: ready becomes in-progress when an attempt begins; blocked and parked are honest branches, and both return only to ready — a blocked leaf is never nearly-done, and a parked leaf keeps its context instead of pretending progress. The two green edges are the whole point of the act: both carry the same label, an accepted receipt exists, because status: done requires accepted: true. Then the red pseudo-node: status: sealed is crossed out — sealing is authorization metadata from the PRE act, it is not backlog state, and the enum refuses it. deep dive S40 · plate 40 of 66 · THE LIFECYCLE — Ready to done

Sealed is not a column, and done is not a mood.

A backlog column is not a feeling — this page explains the small state machine that decides where a leaf may move, and the single condition that guards done.

Five states matter on the plate. ready means dispatchable: nothing is running, the leaf can be handed to an executor. When an attempt begins, the leaf moves to in-progress. From there the two branches are honest ones: blocked when the work waits on a decision someone owes, parked when it is deliberately set aside with its context kept. Both names are chosen to say exactly why the work is not moving — and both return only to ready: a blocked leaf is never nearly-done, and a parked leaf resumes instead of pretending progress. There is no “almost done” column, and no penalty box that quietly decays into completion.

Two edges enter done, and both carry the same label: accepted receipt exists. The rule underneath is one line — status: done requires accepted: true. The transition tool validates the status enum and enforces that acceptance condition on entry to done, so there is no route from worker enthusiasm to done. The only ticket in is the AcceptanceRecord from the previous page.

Just as important is what the map refuses to contain. status: sealed is crossed out in red because sealing is authorization metadata, not backlog state — it was written before the work, at PRE, and it never becomes a column a leaf can sit in. The diagram deliberately separates authorization metadata from backlog state, which is why this page exists.

One more discipline: read the map as the common route, not a full edge whitelist. The tool enforces the enum and the done condition; the plate does not claim to enumerate every legal transition. What it guarantees is the part that matters — blocked and parked lead back to ready, and nothing reaches done without an accepted receipt.

How to read the plate
  • ready → in-progress is the attempt beginning; it is the ordinary route into work.
  • blocked and parked are honest branches, and each returns only to ready — never sideways into done.
  • The two green edges into done share one label: accepted receipt exists.
  • The red dashed pseudo-node is status: sealed — the enum refuses it, because sealing is not a lifecycle state.
Why this page exists

It separates authorization metadata from backlog state, so “done” becomes a settled, receipt-backed fact — not a status anyone can type into a file.

deep dive S41 · plate 41 of 66 · THE FORMAT — Stable core, opt-in evidence

Add proof around the core. Never move it.

Formats usually evolve by breaking their predecessors — this page explains how Task-Spec adds an entire evidence layer without touching the authority split you already trust.

The left card is the stable core, everything format v3 already ships: the atomic leaf with its six zones, behavior↔eval traceability so every promise has a witness, the TaskRevision + HMAC seal, handoff and acceptance, and the deterministic eval path. That is the deterministic loop the last several pages closed — and nothing on this card is deprecated.

The right card is what v4 adds, and every row is opt-in: an explicit evaluation policy, an environment contract, evaluator identity and trust, sealed authoring evidence refs, and attempt-bound external receipts. The pattern is strictly additive: v4 wraps the same core in stronger evidence policy for attempts whose judges live outside the repository. No row removes a v3 obligation — each sits alongside the core, declared in the same frontmatter the leaf already carries.

The load-bearing sentence is that v4 never moves the authority split. Authorization still happens before work, at PRE; acceptance still happens after, at POST. That split — who seals, who executes, who accepts — is the invariant every format version must preserve. v4 changes what kinds of evidence POST can read, not who may authorize and not what may close. And because formats 1–4 remain readable, an older spec never becomes garbage: the toolchain reads what you wrote years ago.

Read the two cards as one promise: evolution without replacement. A leaf that never needs an external evaluator stays on v3 forever and loses nothing; a leaf judged by an outside grader or a named human opts into v4 and gains receipts the deterministic core could not express. The next page opens the first addition — the declaration of what kind of judgment an eval represents.

How to read the plate
  • The left cyan card is what already ships in the deterministic core — the baseline of trust.
  • The right purple card is opt-in; every row is prefixed “+” because nothing is taken away.
  • The footer carries the guarantee: formats 1–4 remain readable, and v3 is not deprecated.
Key detail

v4 adds proof around the same authority split, never through it — the default path is unchanged unless a leaf opts in.

Judge
the evaluator · who or what judges?

Four policies, four trust questions.

v4 makes the leaf say what kind of judgment its eval represents. Each policy answers a different trust question, with a different judge and a different way to be fooled — so deterministic, holdout, graded, and human evidence are not interchangeable, and a receipt from one can never stand in for another.

Story: the first thing v4 adds is a declaration of judgment — the leaf says which kind of judge its evals represent. Read each card as a question, not a feature. Deterministic: did a reproducible assertion pass — the machine judges, and the proof is the rerun. Holdout: did private sealed cases pass without entering the worker context — trust comes from separation, because the attempt cannot overfit to cases it never saw. Graded: did an external evaluator meet a bound rubric and threshold — the rubric is fixed in advance and the judge is not the worker. Human: did the named human approve the bound subject — scoped to this attempt, never a blanket sign-off. The qualifier to land: these four are not interchangeable; a holdout receipt cannot impersonate a human one, and the policy on the leaf decides which receipts POST will even look at.
