deep dive S42 · plate 42 of 66 · THE EVALUATOR — Who or what judges?

Before you trust the verdict, name the judge.

“The eval passed” hides the only question that matters — who or what judged, and why should you believe them?

v4's first addition is a declaration: the leaf says which evaluation policy its evals represent. A policy is a promise about provenance — it tells POST what kind of evidence to expect before any evidence arrives. There are four, and each answers a different trust question, with a different judge and a different way to be fooled. The plate reads them as questions rather than features, because the question is what you are actually trusting.

Deterministic asks: did a reproducible assertion pass? The machine is the judge and the proof is the rerun — the same script gives the same answer anywhere. Holdout asks: did private sealed cases pass without entering the worker's context? Its trust comes from separation — the attempt cannot be fitted to tests it never saw, which closes the overfitting hole that a visible test suite leaves open.

Graded asks: did an external evaluator meet a bound rubric and threshold? The rubric is fixed in advance and the judge is not the worker — judgment comes from outside, but its terms are pinned before the attempt begins. Human asks: did the named human approve the bound subject? A named person accepts a bound subject, recorded as evidence and scoped to this attempt — never a blanket sign-off.

The discipline that makes the taxonomy worth anything: the four are not interchangeable. A holdout receipt cannot impersonate a human one, and a deterministic rerun cannot stand in for a graded rubric — each policy exists because its judge can be fooled in a way the others cannot. The policy on the leaf decides which receipts POST will even look at. And every non-deterministic verdict must bind to the same subject, which is the next page's mechanism.

How to read the plate
  • Four equal cards, one question each — equality is the point: no policy outranks another by default.
  • Distinct icons and colors mark distinct judges — machine, sealed cases, external evaluator, named human.
  • The footer states the rule: receipts are not interchangeable across policies.
Why this page exists

It prepares the receipt taxonomy: once the leaf declares its policy, POST knows which receipts count — and which kinds of trust each one carries.

Bound
the subject · six things must match

ReceiptSubject/v1 prevents evidence replay.

External evidence is valid only for this task, revision, authorization, attempt, base, and closure context — six fields, bound together in one subject. So a valid signature on the wrong attempt still fails: the receipt proves its judge signed something, and the subject proves it was signed about this.

ReceiptSubject/v1 · the binding every receipt must name
{ "contract": "ReceiptSubject/v1", "task_id": "T-…", "task_revision": "sha256:…", "authorization_ref": "hmac-sha256-v3:…", "attempt_id": "uuid", "base_commit": "git-sha", "closure_digest": "sha256:…" }
replay fails A valid signature over the wrong attempt still fails — evidence cannot travel between attempts. Different observers can now contribute evidence without becoming the task authority.
Story: ReceiptSubject/v1 is the anti-replay device, and it exists because signatures alone are not enough. Walk the six chips: task id, task revision, authorization ref, attempt id, base commit, closure digest — each sends one rail, and all six converge on a single receipt that is bound to exactly this subject. A receipt is valid only when every field matches the attempt being accepted; the hexagonal binding on the right is not decoration, it is the whole mechanism. So the failure mode to name out loud: a perfectly valid Ed25519 signature over the wrong attempt still fails — evidence cannot be carried from one attempt into another, and last month's green cannot cosign this month's patch. deep dive S43 · plate 43 of 66 · THE SUBJECT — Six things must match

A genuine signature, aimed at the wrong attempt, still fails.

A valid signature proves someone signed something — this page explains the six-field binding that proves they signed about this attempt.

External evidence has a replay problem. Suppose a graded receipt was honestly signed last month for an earlier attempt: the signature verifies perfectly. Without a binding, nothing stops that old green from being presented again for today's patch. Cryptography alone cannot fix this, because the signature is genuine — it is just genuine about the wrong thing.

ReceiptSubject/v1 is the fix: six fields bound together in one object that every external receipt must name. task_id — this leaf. task_revision — this sealed revision of the contract. authorization_ref — this authorization. attempt_id — this execution. base_commit — this Git base. closure_digest — this frozen environment and closure context. Each field pins a different axis of identity: the first three pin the authority, the attempt id pins the run, and the last two pin the world the run started from.

The rule is all six or nothing: a receipt is valid only when every field matches the attempt being accepted. A valid Ed25519 signature over the wrong attempt still fails. Evidence cannot travel between attempts, between revisions, or between bases — last month's green cannot cosign this month's patch, and a receipt minted against a different closure cannot witness this one. The check is deliberately mechanical: six comparisons, and all six must pass.

This is what makes the next page possible. Without the subject, a fan-in of external evidence would be a free-for-all — any signed statement from any reviewer could be offered for any attempt. With it, different observers — a holdout harness, an external grader, a named human — can contribute evidence about one attempt without any of them becoming the task authority. The observers multiply; the thing they observe stays singular.

How to read the plate
  • The six chips are the fields — gold for sealed authority, purple for the attempt, cyan for base and closure.
  • The hexagonal binding is the mechanism, not decoration: all six rails converge on one receipt.
  • The red caption is the whole rule — any field mismatches and the receipt is refused.
Key detail

Replay fails because signature validity is checked over the subject — and the subject names exactly one task, revision, authorization, attempt, base, and closure.

the evidence · many receipts, one acceptance

deep dive S44 · plate 44 of 66 · THE EVIDENCE — Many receipts, one acceptance

Observers multiply. Authorizers do not.

More evidence should mean more confidence, not more cooks — this page explains how five kinds of receipts converge on one verdict while authority stays exactly where it was sealed.

The fan-in: five receipt types flow into POST. The holdout receipt from sealed cases that never entered the worker's context, the graded receipt from an external evaluator against a bound rubric, the human receipt from a named person accepting a bound subject, the environment receipt with host-signed structural proof of the world, and the engine run receipt from the deterministic eval run itself. Every one is bound to the same ReceiptSubject from the previous page — and because each observer sees a different facet of the attempt, their conjunction is worth more than any single verdict.

The sixth input is not a receipt at all: EvaluatorTrust/v1, the configuration of belief — which evaluators POST will accept receipts from, and under which keys. The signature rule is strict: portable or human-authorized non-deterministic receipts require external Ed25519 trust, the evaluator's own key bound in that policy — never the worker's self-report.

All six rails converge on one POST policy node, and the output is still one AcceptanceRecord/v1 of one shape. Keep that sentence: more evidence never means more verdicts, and never a new kind of verdict. That is why the output card is drawn in gold — it is the same receipt object the earlier plate pinned field by field, not an evidence-flavored variant. Observability goes up; the acceptance object stays singular and attempt-bound, exactly as the deterministic core wrote it.

Then the gold rail along the bottom — the one the headline is about. The task authorization sealed at PRE rides straight into the acceptance record, bypassing the fan-in entirely and unchanged no matter how many receipts arrive. Trust configuration can widen or tighten who may observe; it cannot mint authority. Adding observers never adds authorizers: evidence fans in, authority does not fan out.

How to read the plate
  • The five receipt cards are the observers — one per evidence kind, all subject-bound.
  • The purple EvaluatorTrust/v1 card configures which evaluators POST will believe.
  • The green POST node reads everything; the gold output card is the same AcceptanceRecord/v1 as before.
  • The bottom gold rail carries the PRE-sealed authorization past the fan-in, untouched by the evidence count.
Why this page exists

It shows v4 strengthening observability without redistributing authority — the acceptance object and the authorization rail are both unchanged.

Risk
the trust boundary · what still can go wrong

Proof is scoped. Risk stays explicit.

Every control in this deck was built to kill a named failure mode — and each one leaves a named residue behind. Read the rows left to right: what the control eliminates, and what it honestly does not. Controls eliminate named failure modes; they do not eliminate judgment.

deep dive S45 · plate 45 of 66 · THE TRUST BOUNDARY — What still can go wrong

The inventory of what this system does not prove.

A system that cannot say what it does not prove will eventually oversell what it does — this page is the honest inventory, taken before anyone builds on top.

Every control in this book was built to kill a named failure mode, and the plate pairs each one with the residual risk it honestly leaves behind. Read each row left to right: what the control eliminates, then what remains. Nothing on the right column is a flaw in the design — it is the design, stated accurately. Each residue is a place where a person or an eval still has to be right; the contract makes those places visible instead of pretending they are gone.

Walk the rows. HMAC v3 detects mutation of the canonical TaskRevision — but a shared-key holder can still authorize bad work; the seal proves integrity, not wisdom. Behavior↔eval traceability guarantees every promise has a witness — but the behavior or the eval can be weak. An Ed25519 receipt proves who signed and about which subject — not that the evaluator was right, or uncompromised.

The blast-radius check keeps the patch inside the sealed write surface — but in-scope changes can still be harmful; scope is not goodness. An environment receipt is host-signed structural proof — and structural proof may not equal deployed behavior. A human receipt puts a named person on the record — and the human can make a bad decision.

The core line, kept exactly: controls eliminate named failure modes; they do not eliminate judgment. The closing promise of the whole system is inspectable authority and proof — not guaranteed success. That honesty, stated before the machinery arrives, is what earns the next act: with authority and proof explicitly bounded, an optional runtime can safely move more than one leaf at a time.

How to read the plate
  • Left column — the controls, in cyan and green: each one eliminates a named failure mode.
  • The red arrows are the honesty gap between what a control kills and what it leaves.
  • Right column — the residue, in red: the risk that remains after the control has done its job.
  • No row claims judgment was eliminated — that absence is the point of the page.
The boundary

This page is the credibility gate before orchestration: the claims stop here, on purpose, so the next act starts from ground that does not overpromise.

deep dive S46 · plate 46 of 66 · THE BOUNDARY — Two products

One product decides. The other only moves.

Before any architecture, this page draws the custody line between the two products this book ships: Task-Spec decides what work is authorized and what counts as done; TaskMesh coordinates the running of it — and may never cross the line.

Task-Spec, the gold plate on the left, is the canonical task authority. It owns the graph and the ready frontier, the PRE and POST gates, the acceptance record, and — always — the human-owned topology and the target merge. TaskMesh, the purple plate on the right, is an optional local execution control plane: it holds leases and waves, routes and observes attempts, and manages worktrees plus one integration branch. Coordination is a service it performs; authority is a property it lacks.

The core line is a list of things the right plate cannot do. TaskMesh consumes the canonical Tier-1 frontier — it cannot widen it. It cannot rewrite a signed leaf. It cannot accept on its own terms, and it never mutates the target branch. These are not feature gaps; they are the design. An optional helper that could widen scope or accept work would be an authorizer, and this system already has one.

The two rails between the plates are the entire interface. Outward, in cyan: TaskGraphView/v1 and TaskHandoff/v3 — the derived frontier and the authorized attempt, handed over. Inward, in green: ordered events and attempt evidence, flowing back into the record. Nothing else crosses in either direction.

Hold the plate's own summary: authority verbs live on the left, motion verbs on the right. Every mechanism in this act — leases, routing, worktrees, cockpits — is one of the motion verbs, and each is audited against the rule that the left plate never delegates the decision of what may run or what may close.

How to read the plate
  • The gold plate is Task-Spec — contract and receipt; every authority verb lives here.
  • The purple plate is TaskMesh — the optional control plane; every motion verb lives here.
  • The cyan rail carries TaskGraphView/v1 and TaskHandoff/v3 outward — the only inputs the mesh may take.
  • The green rail returns ordered events and attempt evidence — the only output it may give.
  • The table is the custody split, row by row — memorize one row and the rest follow.
Why this page exists

Every TaskMesh plate that follows is judged against this boundary. If a mechanism ever looks like it widens scope, rewrites a signed leaf, or accepts work, it has been misread — the mesh moves authorized work; it never redefines it.

Plane
the taskmesh · system architecture

One local daemon, many cockpits.

Every cockpit — Codex, Claude, Grok, or MCP — talks to the same repository-local Go daemon through a thin Python shim. The daemon keeps durable ordered events in SQLite WAL, derives the frontier, fences leases, owns the worktrees, and routes deterministically to four adapters. The work always ends where it began: at the canonical taskspec accept.

durable core, thin edges Cockpits come and go; the daemon and its event history stay. The shim exists so the optional helper can fail closed before any run.
Story: this is the map for the whole act, so walk it left to right. Three cockpits — Codex, Claude, and Grok or MCP — converge on one Python shim, taskspec mesh; the shim speaks TaskMeshAPI/v1alpha1 to a single repository-local Go daemon, taskspec-meshd. Below the daemon sits SQLite WAL holding ordered events — that pairing is why a cockpit can disconnect and another can reconnect to the same run. From the daemon, four rails fan out: the canonical TaskGraphView/v1 frontier comes in, leases plus fencing keep one attempt authoritative, run and attempt worktrees isolate the Git side, and the deterministic router picks an adapter — Codex native, Claude native, Grok native, or OMP RPC. Land on the gold node: everything still ends at the canonical taskspec accept; the mesh never accepts on its own. deep dive S47 · plate 47 of 66 · THE TASKMESH — System architecture

Cockpits are disposable. The daemon is not.

This is the map for the whole act: every cockpit you might drive — Codex, Claude, Grok, or MCP — talks to one durable, repository-local daemon, and this page shows every road in and out of it.

Read the graph left to right. The three cockpits converge on a thin Python shim, taskspec mesh, which speaks one versioned protocol — TaskMeshAPI/v1alpha1 — to taskspec-meshd, a Go daemon that runs once per repository. Cockpits and shim are thin, replaceable edges; the daemon is the only stateful component in the picture.

Below the daemon sits its memory: SQLite in WAL mode, holding ordered events. That pairing is why a cockpit can disconnect and another can reconnect to the same run — the truth lives in the log, not in any window. The daemon listens on a private Unix socket (0600) and treats requests as idempotent, so a retried call cannot double-apply. The daemon is also the only writer to that log, which keeps the ordering total — every event has exactly one position, so two cockpits can never disagree about what happened.

From the daemon, four rails fan out, and they are its four jobs. TaskGraphView/v1 brings the canonical frontier in. Leases + fencing keep at most one attempt authoritative. Run + attempt worktrees isolate the Git side. The deterministic router picks an executor from four adapters — Codex native, Claude native, Grok native, OMP RPC. Notice what the adapters hang off: the router, never the daemon directly — every dispatch passes through one explainable funnel.

The graph ends where authority lives: the worktrees rail terminates at the gold canonical taskspec accept node. Execution can be delegated into the mesh; acceptance cannot — POST stays the gate, outside it. Keep this map open in your head: each plate that follows zooms into exactly one node or rail on it.

How to read the plate
  • Cockpits and shim are the thin edges — any window can be swapped or closed.
  • The glowing daemon is the only stateful node — one per repository.
  • SQLite WAL is the durable history every view is replayed from.
  • The four fan-out rails are the daemon's four jobs — frontier, fencing, worktrees, routing.
  • The gold node sits outside the mesh — canonical acceptance remains the gate.
Why this page exists

An act with leases, waves, routes, and worktrees needs a stable map before any detail. Every later plate names its node here first — shim, daemon, state machine, wave, router, lease, worktree, adapter, cockpit.

Shim
the shim · optional means fail-closed

The handshake happens before any run.

Because TaskMesh is optional, its absence is a first-class outcome, not a crash. The shim negotiates an exact version match with the daemon before anything moves: a core-only install explains how to add TaskMesh, and a mismatched helper returns a stable runtime error — never a silent fallback.

fail-closed at the boundary Optionality is enforced at the executable seam, not promised in prose. Once negotiated, every runtime object is typed.
Story: before any architecture detail matters, the optional helper has to prove it is the right helper. The two cards shake hands on one green rail: taskspec 3.9.0 core meets taskspec-meshd 3.9.0, and only an exact match closes the circuit. The gold chip underneath is the runtime floor — exit 3 for an unsupported runtime, the same floor the core CLI uses. Then the two red branches: if the helper is missing, the shim returns TASKMESH_ERROR=MESH_UNAVAILABLE and the core-only install explains how to add TaskMesh; if the versions disagree, TASKMESH_ERROR=MESH_VERSION_MISMATCH comes back as a stable, greppable runtime error. The qualifier: there is no third branch — no silent fallback, no partial negotiation, no automatic upgrade. Sources: [I] src/meshctl/cli.py, mesh/cmd/taskspec-meshd/main.go; [E] tests/test-mesh-contracts.sh. Transition: once negotiated, every runtime object is typed.
deep dive S48 · plate 48 of 66 · THE SHIM — Optional means fail-closed

Optionality you can test at the shell.

Because TaskMesh is optional, its absence has to be a designed outcome — this page shows the handshake that runs before any work, and the only two ways it is allowed to fail.

The two cards are two executables. taskspec 3.9.0, the Python core, is always present and works alone. taskspec-meshd 3.9.0, the Go helper, is optional — but if it is present, it must match exactly. Before anything moves, the shim negotiates that version match; only then does the green rail close. This is why the shim exists at all: so the optional helper can fail closed before any run, while the core stays untouched.

The first red branch is the missing helper. Nothing crashes: the shim returns TASKMESH_ERROR=MESH_UNAVAILABLE, and the core-only install explains how to add TaskMesh — then keeps working without it. Absence is a first-class outcome with its own message, not an exception.

The second red branch is disagreement. A version mismatch returns TASKMESH_ERROR=MESH_VERSION_MISMATCH — a stable, greppable runtime error a pipeline can branch on. Under both branches sits the runtime floor the core CLI already uses: exit 3 for an unsupported runtime. These tokens are contract, not mood — they are covered by the mesh contract tests. Exact match also means there is no version skew to debug: the helper is either the same release as the core or it is refused. And the guidance branch matters as much as the error branch — it is the difference between a tool you can adopt gradually and one you must install before anything works.

What matters most is what is missing from the page: no silent fallback, no partial negotiation, no automatic upgrade. Optional means fail-closed — the helper proves it is the right helper before any run, or the system refuses in a way you can script against. That is product separation enforced at the executable seam, not promised in prose.

How to read the plate
  • The two cards are the two executables — core always present, helper optional.
  • The green rail closes only on an exact version match — 3.9.0 to 3.9.0.
  • The gold chip is the runtime floor — exit 3, the same floor the core CLI uses.
  • The two red branches are the only allowed failures — helper missing, versions mismatched.
Why this page exists

This is where product separation stops being a claim. Either the handshake succeeds, or you get a named, stable error — the mesh cannot smuggle itself into a core-only install.

the mesh contracts · observable state

Every mesh object is typed and readable.

The control plane keeps no hidden state: the run, the capability, the route, the lease, the event, the view, the sandbox, the credential, and the roster are all versioned, machine-readable contracts. That is what makes TaskMesh inspectable and reconnectable — any cockpit can read the same objects and see the same truth.

no hidden state Nine contracts, all readable, all versioned. Those objects describe a run that survives the cockpit.

Row one is the lifecycle spine: the TaskMeshRun, the ExecutorCapability an adapter declares, and the DispatchDecision that retains the whole route. deep dive S49 · plate 49 of 66 · THE MESH CONTRACTS — Observable state

Nine nouns, no hidden state.

Everything the control plane knows is written down as a versioned, machine-readable object — this page is the complete vocabulary, and there is nothing behind it.

At the top sits the hub: TaskMeshAPI/v1alpha1, the one versioned protocol every cockpit speaks. Around it, the nine contracts the protocol moves. Row one is the lifecycle spine: the TaskMeshRun — which wave, which attempts, which state; the ExecutorCapability an adapter declares up front; the DispatchDecision that retains the entire route.

Row two is authority and history: the RunLease carrying exclusive attempt authority with its fencing token; the TaskMeshEvent, one ordered fact in the durable log; the TaskMeshView, the reconstructed state any cockpit can read. Row three is the trust material: host-signed SandboxEvidence, the expiring CredentialLease, and the TaskMeshRoster mapping effort bands to named models.

Typed objects are what make the control plane inspectable and reconnectable. There is no private daemon memory to take on trust: any cockpit reads the same schemas and sees the same truth, and a view can be rebuilt after a crash precisely because events are themselves one of the nine contracts. That is also what makes the contracts observable state rather than API surface: the state is the objects, all of them, all the time — nothing is computed behind the glass. And the DispatchDecision from row one deserves a pause: it retains not just the winner but every candidate, rejection, preference, and tie-break — routing you can cross-examine later.

Each card names its schema file — spec/schemas/taskmesh-*.schema.json — so every noun on this page is a file you can open, diff, and validate against, and the reference docs mirror the same nine names one to one. The mesh's state is observable by construction, which is exactly what lets a run survive the cockpit that started it.

How to read the plate
  • The hub is one versioned protocol — TaskMeshAPI/v1alpha1.
  • Row one runs the lifecycle — run, capability, dispatch decision.
  • Row two holds authority and history — lease, event, view.
  • Row three carries trust — sandbox evidence, credential lease, roster.
  • The filename on each card is the schema you can open and read.
Key detail

Because the view is a contract among contracts, reconnecting is a read, not a recovery ritual — replay the events, rebuild the TaskMeshView, and two different cockpits see identical state.

Replay
the daemon · replay, not memory

Durable history lives with the repository.

The daemon writes ordered events to SQLite WAL; the view you see is a replay of that log, not process memory. Kill the cockpit or restart the daemon and the same TaskMeshView is rebuilt — identical run IDs, identical state, with no hosted control plane anywhere in the loop.

repository-scoped identity private runtime directory unix socket 0600 idempotent request IDs
no hosted control plane Continuity across cockpits comes from a file next to the repo, not a service. The event history records a strict attempt state machine.

Walk the cyan rail: five ordered events — run created, lease issued at fence 8, attempt started, eval passed, view updated — all appended to SQLite WAL. Then the red crash tick: kill the cockpit, restart the daemon, it does not matter; the TaskMeshView on the right is replayed from the log. deep dive S50 · plate 50 of 66 · THE DAEMON — Replay, not memory

Restart anything. Lose nothing.

The daemon's memory is a file that lives next to your repository — so killing a cockpit, or the daemon itself, is an inconvenience, never a loss.

The mechanism is a replay log. Every fact — run.created, lease.issued at fence 8, attempt.started, eval.passed, view.updated — is appended as an ordered event to SQLite in WAL mode, and write-ahead logging means the event hits durable storage before anyone sees its effect. What a cockpit displays is a replay of that log: the TaskMeshView is derived from events, not held in process memory.

Walk the plate left to right. The cyan rail accumulates events; the red tick is a crash — client or daemon, it does not matter which; the card after it is the same view rebuilt from the log. The payoff is the equals sign below: the Codex window before the restart and the Claude window after it show the same run-42, the same attempt B, the same verifying state.

The chips carry the posture that makes a repository-local daemon safe to run: repository-scoped identity, a private runtime directory, a Unix socket at 0600, and idempotent request IDs so a retried command cannot double-apply. Continuity here needs no account, no server, no network.

Hold the boundary the footer implies: replay gives you continuity, not authority. Rebuilding a view never re-accepts work — acceptance still belongs to the canonical gate — and there is no hosted control plane anywhere in the loop. This is a local control plane whose entire memory is a file you can inspect or delete. Deleting it deletes the mesh's memory and nothing else — the repository and the canonical record are untouched. And because every request is idempotent, a cockpit that retries after a flaky moment cannot corrupt the log: the same request ID lands once.

How to read the plate
  • The event chips are the facts, in order — each an append to the WAL log.
  • The red tick is any crash — cockpit or daemon, either survives.
  • The replayed view is derived state — identical because the log is identical.
  • The two windows are the proof — different cockpits, same run ID and state.
Why this page exists

Cross-cockpit continuity is usually a hosted service's job. Here it comes from a file next to the repo — which is exactly why a cockpit can disappear and the run cannot.

States
the run · state machine

An attempt moves through explicit states.

Execution, verification, supervision, acceptance, and integration are separate transitions, each one an event in the log. The happy path runs eligible through integrated; every failure is a named side state — lost, cancelled, rejected, parked — never a silent disappearance.

not lifecycle authority An attempt state is not Task-Spec lifecycle authority — canonical acceptance remains the gate. Before leasing, TaskMesh computes one safe wave from the canonical frontier.
Story: the event log from the last slide records this machine. Walk the main chain left to right: eligible means the frontier said ready; leased means a fencing token was issued; preparing builds the worktree and evidence; running hands the attempt to an adapter; verifying reruns the evals; accepted is the canonical POST gate from Act V; integrated means merged into the run branch. Between verifying and accepted sits awaiting supervision — a dashed node on purpose, a human checkpoint, not an automatic step. Below are the side exits: lost from leased or running when heartbeats stop, cancelled when the supervisor stops it, rejected when POST refuses, parked when a conflict forces a safe halt. The qualifier on the strip must survive: an attempt state is not Task-Spec lifecycle authority — canonical acceptance remains the gate. Sources: [N/I] spec/schemas/taskmesh-run.schema.json, mesh/internal/mesh/types.go, store.go. Transition: before leasing, TaskMesh computes one safe wave from the canonical frontier.
deep dive S51 · plate 51 of 66 · THE RUN — State machine

Every way an attempt can end has a name.

An attempt's life is a small state machine, drawn in full on this page — every transition is an event in the log, and every failure lands in a named state instead of disappearing.

Walk the happy path. eligible means the canonical frontier says the leaf is ready. leased means a fencing token was issued. preparing builds the worktree and evidence. running hands the attempt to an adapter. verifying reruns the evals. accepted is the canonical POST gate, and integrated means merged into the run branch. Each verb is one transition, and each transition is one row in the event history.

Between verifying and accepted sits awaiting_supervision, drawn dashed on purpose: a human checkpoint, not an automatic step. Verification can route an attempt through a person's eyes before the gate, and the machine records that pause like any other transition. An attempt that sits there simply waits — the state makes the waiting visible instead of silent. And no arrow skips a state on the chain, just as no side state is reachable from nowhere.

The four side states are the honest failures. lost — reachable from leased or running — when a heartbeat stops. cancelled — from running — when the supervisor stops it. rejected — from verifying — when POST refuses. parked — from running — when a conflict forces a safe halt. Follow the arrows: each exit names exactly which states can reach it, and each is a state with its own events. Nothing vanishes silently.

The qualifier on the strip is load-bearing: an attempt state is not Task-Spec lifecycle authority. The mesh can say an attempt ran; only canonical acceptance — after the work, at the POST gate — decides what may close. Execution, verification, supervision, acceptance, and integration are separate transitions precisely so that each can be gated, logged, and refused on its own.

How to read the plate
  • The main chain runs left to right — seven states, each a logged transition.
  • The dashed node is awaiting_supervision — a human checkpoint by design.
  • The side states are explicit failures — lost, cancelled, rejected, parked.
  • The arrows into them name the reaching states — leased and running, running, verifying, running.
The boundary

Accepted sits on the chain, but it is not the mesh's decision — it is the canonical POST gate from the previous act. TaskMesh observes the verdict; it never issues one.

Wave
the wave · frontier to parallel work

A wave is only authorized, disjoint leaves.

Parallelism starts from the canonical TaskGraphView frontier and then only shrinks. Five filters — leaf, ready, Tier 1 current, dependency closure stable, write-disjoint — remove anything the seal or the graph cannot vouch for. What survives is the first deterministic concurrency group: work that may run side by side without ever touching the same files.

shrink-only scheduling A filter can only remove a leaf, never promote one. Eligibility narrows the set; routing chooses one executor without expanding it.
Story: this is where graph semantics become scheduling. On the left is the canonical input — the TaskGraphView/v1 ready frontier, nine leaves visible. Then the funnel does its work: leaf drops composition nodes, ready drops blocked work, Tier 1 current refuses stale seals, closure stable detects drift in the dependency world, and write-disjoint holds back anything whose moat overlaps a sibling. Watch the counts narrow from nine to three; a filter can only remove, never promote. On the right, the survivors fan out as the first deterministic concurrency group — three parallel lanes, each on its own worktree with its own fence. The qualifier: this is derived scheduling over an already-authorized frontier; the wave never creates eligibility. Sources: [I] mesh/internal/mesh/graph.go, routing.go; [E] tests/test-mesh-leases.sh. Transition: eligibility narrows the set; routing chooses one executor without expanding it.
deep dive S52 · plate 52 of 66 · THE WAVE — Frontier to parallel work

Parallelism is what survives five refusals.

This page shows how the mesh turns the canonical frontier into parallel work — by removing everything it cannot vouch for, and never by promoting anything.

The input on the left is the TaskGraphView/v1 ready frontier — derived from the canonical Markdown and Git graph, and never widened by the mesh. Nine leaves are visible; the question the wave answers is which of them may run at the same time. Nothing enters the funnel from anywhere else — the mesh cannot add a leaf the graph did not already call ready.

The five filters answer it, and the survivor counts tell the story. Leaf drops composition nodes — XL/XXL work waits to be decomposed. Ready drops leaves whose dependencies are unsatisfied. Tier 1 · current refuses stale seals — authorization must verify now. Closure stable detects drift in the dependency world. Write-disjoint holds back any leaf whose write set overlaps a sibling's. Nine becomes seven, then five, then three. Read the counts as the funnel's honesty: a filter that removes nothing still says so — five stays five — because a stable check is information, not a failure, and the next wave can re-run the same filters over a changed graph.

What emerges on the right is the first deterministic concurrency group: three lanes — attempts A, B, C — each on its own worktree with its own fence. Deterministic means the same frontier always yields the same wave, so the schedule is reproducible, not improvised. A leaf that misses this wave simply waits for the next one.

The discipline that makes this safe is that eligibility only shrinks: a filter can remove a leaf, never promote one. The wave is derived scheduling over an already-authorized frontier — graph semantics turned directly into safe concurrency, with the luminous rails showing the one direction the flow can go.

How to read the plate
  • The cyan frontier card is the canonical input — derived, never widened.
  • The five filter cards are the refusals in order; the counts narrow nine to three.
  • The luminous rails show the flow's one direction — frontier, through filters, to lanes.
  • The three green lanes are the wave — disjoint leaves, each fenced and worktreed.
Key detail

Write-disjoint is the filter that makes concurrency safe: two leaves that touch the same files can both be eligible, but never in the same wave — the later one waits.

Route
the router · deterministic and explainable

Routing may rank. It may not invent.

Choosing an executor is a recorded funnel, not a judgment call: eligibility first, then explicit override, the leaf's declared backend, roster preference, a bounded advisor reorder, and a stable tie-break. Every candidate, rejection, preference, reorder, and tie-break is retained in the DispatchDecision — the route can be explained line by line afterward.

step 1 · entry set
Eligible capabilities
from the roster + adapter manifests — ineligible names are rejected with reasons, not skipped quietly
step 2 · human wins
Explicit adapter override

deep dive S53 · plate 53 of 66 · THE ROUTER — Deterministic and explainable

A route you can cross-examine.

When the mesh picks an executor for a leaf, the choice is not a judgment call — it is a recorded funnel of six steps, and every step is kept.

Read the funnel top to bottom. It starts from eligible capabilities declared by the roster and the adapter manifests — ineligible names are rejected with reasons, not skipped quietly. An explicit --adapter override wins first, because the human outranks the heuristic. Then the leaf's own execution_backend narrows the field — the contract speaks before any preference does. That order is deliberate: authority flows from the human, then the leaf, then the roster.

Next, the effort/kind roster preference ranks what remains. A bounded advisor may then reorder the surviving candidates — reshuffle, nothing more. Equal ranks fall to a stable adapter-order tie-break: same inputs, same route, every time. No step may widen the field — each can only narrow or rank it. Preferences never override eligibility; they only order what survived. The wave decided what may run; this funnel decides who runs it — and because the tie-break is a fixed adapter order, two runs over the same inputs pick the same executor.

The terminal node is the point of the page: DispatchDecision/v1 persists every candidate, rejection, preference, advisor reorder, and tie-break. Ask afterward why an adapter ran and the answer is a record you can read line by line — not a shrug, and not a log you have to reconstruct. Deterministic plus retained equals explainable.

The red callout is the advisor's cage: it cannot add an unknown or ineligible adapter. Anything it suggests is checked against the same eligibility set, and a suggestion that fails is refused — and the refusal is recorded like everything else. The advisor shuffles a fixed deck; it never deals new cards.

How to read the plate
  • The funnel's order is the priority — human override, the leaf, preference, advisor, arithmetic.
  • Eligibility comes first — every later step only narrows or ranks survivors.
  • The green terminal is the retained DispatchDecision/v1, not just a winner.
  • The red boundary caps the advisor — reorder only, never invent.
Why this page exists

Routing is where an automation system usually hides its judgment. Here the judgment is flattened into a fixed order and an auditable record — the route can be explained, so it can be trusted.

deep dive S54 · plate 54 of 66 · THE ROSTER — Current head, not frozen proof

A real feature with an honest label.

Current main can route attempts by named models — this page shows the roster feature and, with equal weight, the two reasons you may not treat it as frozen 3.9.0 release proof.

The feature first. A TaskMeshRoster/v1 can map effort bands and kinds to named models: the window shows bands like XS-S and M-L, each carrying candidate adapter-plus-model pairs. An explicit --model always wins over the band, and require_named_model fails closed when no name resolves — an unnamed resolution is a refusal, not a guess. Routing stays inside the eligible set; the roster only names which model an eligible adapter should run.

Now the first qualifier. The schema also carries mode and failover fields, but at the audited commit those fields are parsed, not consumed by runtime routing. Parsed means the file loads; consumed would mean the runtime acts on it — the distance between those two verbs is exactly the size of the qualifier. So this book never promises semantic mode or failover behavior.

The second qualifier is about evidence. The frozen 3.9.0 corridor predates this change, so named-model routing is not part of the immutable release proof. It is current-main behavior, and it wears the gold CURRENT MAIN tag so nobody mistakes it for more. The changelog's [Unreleased] section is the source of truth for what head can do, and a reader who trusts the tag can safely use the feature — a reader who needs frozen proof knows to wait for it.

This is the book's claim discipline applied to itself: honesty about what is proven is part of the product. When the repository head drifts ahead of the frozen evidence, the drift gets a label instead of a silent upgrade — the same rule the mesh applies to leaves, applied to the deck's own claims.

How to read the plate
  • The gold tag is the label — current main, not frozen proof.
  • The JSON window is the roster's real shape at head.
  • require_named_model is fail-closed — no resolved name, no route.
  • The red callout carries both qualifiers — parsed-not-consumed fields, predated evidence.
The boundary

Do not extend this page's claims: no semantic mode or failover promises, and no folding current-main roster behavior into the 3.9.0 corridor. The label is the feature's contract with the reader.

Fence
the lease · monotonic fencing

A higher fence retires a stale attempt.

At most one active lease is authoritative for a task revision. When a heartbeat dies, recovery marks the attempt lost and issues the next lease with a higher fencing token — so when the old worker eventually phones home, its result is refused by number, not by negotiation.

the qualifier
Fencing prevents stale result authority — it does not make model execution exactly-once. The stale attempt may still have run side effects in its own worktree; what it can never do is report them as truth.
authority by number The fence only goes up — a late worker argues with arithmetic and loses. Each fenced attempt also gets its own branch and worktree.
Story: read the sequence top to bottom. The daemon leases attempt A at fence 7 with a TTL. A's heartbeat stops — the red cross — so the daemon marks A lost and issues attempt B a new lease at fence 8. Then the interesting moment: A wakes up and delivers a late result carrying fence 7, and the daemon refuses it — STALE_FENCE — while B's current result at fence 8 is accepted forward. The mechanism is monotonic arithmetic, not judgment: the fence only goes up. The gold callout is the qualifier that must not be lost: fencing prevents stale result authority; it does not make model execution exactly-once — side effects in A's worktree may exist, they just can never be reported as truth. Sources: [I] mesh/internal/mesh/lease.go, recovery.go; [E] tests/test-mesh-leases.sh. Transition: each fenced attempt also gets its own branch and worktree.
deep dive S55 · plate 55 of 66 · THE LEASE — Monotonic fencing

The fence only goes up.

When a worker dies mid-attempt and a replacement takes over, the mesh needs one guarantee: the dead worker can never come back and win. This page shows the number that enforces it.

A RunLease makes at most one active lease authoritative for a task revision, and it carries a fencing token — a number — plus a time-to-live. Attempt A receives fence=7; while its heartbeats arrive, it alone may report results for that revision. The token is issued with the lease and checked with every result. A lease is scoped to one task revision, so re-sealing the task starts a fresh game rather than inheriting the old one. And recovery needs no confession from the dead worker — silence is ambiguous, so the system simply moves on.

Then the heartbeat stops — the red cross. Recovery marks A lost and issues attempt B a new lease with a higher token, fence=8. When A eventually wakes and delivers a late result still carrying fence=7, the daemon compares numbers and refuses it: STALE_FENCE. B's result, carrying the current fence, is accepted forward.

The guarantee is monotonic arithmetic, not negotiation: the fence only ever increases, so a stale holder cannot argue, retry, or race its way back into authority. One comparison settles what ad-hoc recovery logic usually botches. Notice the diagram's geometry, too: the lost-marking and the new lease happen entirely on the daemon's side — no signal to the stale worker is required, because none is trusted.

Hold the qualifier in the gold callout: fencing prevents stale result authority — it does not make model execution exactly-once. Attempt A may have left side effects in its own worktree; what it can never do is report them as truth. Authority is fenced; physics is not. That narrower promise is what the tests prove.

How to read the plate
  • The three lifelines are attempt A, the daemon, and attempt B.
  • The red cross is the stopped heartbeat — the trigger for recovery.
  • fence=7 → fence=8 is the monotonic step — the number never repeats or decreases.
  • The dashed late result is A's comeback, refused by number.
  • The green close is B's current result, accepted forward.
Key detail

Exactly-once execution is not promised anywhere in this system. What is promised is narrower and stronger — at most one authoritative reporter per task revision, enforced by comparison.

Branch
the worktree · branch topology

Attempts merge into a run branch — never the target.

Every run grows its own integration branch, and every fenced attempt works in its own worktree. Accepted attempts merge back into the run branch one by one; the user's target branch stays pinned and untouched until a human chooses to merge.

the refusal
If the target diverges or an accepted attempt conflicts, the run parks safely — the state machine's parked exit — and waits for a human. There is no implicit rebase and no automatic resolution.
isolation in git, not just process Branches are the blast radius. What runs inside those worktrees depends on the execution mode.
Story: the lease from the last slide gets a physical home here. The bottom grey line is the user's target branch — pinned, untouched for the entire run. Above it the purple line is the run's integration branch, taskspec-mesh/run-42, created from that pin. Attempt A branches off into its own worktree, commits leaf A, and merges back as the green accepted A node; attempt B does the same as accepted B. Only accepted work reaches the run branch — a lost or rejected attempt's worktree simply never merges. The red callout is the boundary: target divergence or a merge conflict parks the run safely — no implicit rebase, no automatic resolution, and no target-branch mutation ever. Sources: [I] mesh/internal/mesh/worktree.go, integration.go; [E] tests/test-mesh-routing-integration.sh. Transition: what runs inside those worktrees depends on the execution mode.
deep dive S56 · plate 56 of 66 · THE WORKTREE — Branch topology

The target branch never moves.

Every fenced attempt gets a physical home in Git — this page shows the branch topology that keeps delegated work away from your target branch until a person says otherwise.

The bottom grey line is the user's target branch — pinned and untouched for the entire run. From that pin, the mesh grows one integration branch per run, taskspec-mesh/run-42. Each attempt then branches off into its own worktree — its own working directory on its own branch, so two attempts never share files. The dashed pin line is the only connection the topology ever draws between the two — and it points down, read-only.

Attempt A commits its leaf and, once accepted, merges back into the run branch as the green accepted A node; attempt B follows as accepted B. Only accepted work reaches the integration branch — a lost or rejected attempt's worktree simply never merges, and its stale fence guarantees it cannot force the issue.

The red callout is the failure posture: if the target diverges or an accepted attempt conflicts, the run parks safely — the parked state from the state machine — and waits for a human. There is no implicit rebase and no automatic resolution. Parking is a feature, not a stall: it preserves both branches exactly as they were, so a person can resolve the conflict with full context. The integration branch is simply where the run's accepted work accumulates — one merge per accepted attempt, in order.

This is the Git-side expression of the act's whole discipline: the mesh may move work, but it never advances the target. When the run finishes, what you receive is a human merge route — commands for a person to run — never a shipped branch. Branches are the blast radius: a bad attempt contaminates its own worktree and nothing else.

How to read the plate
  • The grey line is the target branch — pinned, never mutated by the mesh.
  • The purple line is the run's integration branch, grown from that pin.
  • The arcs are attempt worktrees — one per fenced attempt.
  • The green nodes are accepted merges — unaccepted work never lands.
The boundary

Isolation here is structural, not procedural. The target branch does not even know the run happened until a human chooses the merge — divergence and conflict park the run instead of resolving themselves.

Supervised
the adapters · human in the loop

Supervised execution is process separation, not a sandbox.

The four native adapters — Codex, Claude, Grok, OMP — each preserve one handoff and one observable attempt. They differ in command shape and in which capabilities are trimmed, but they share the supervised posture: a human may watch, interrupt, and accept, and nothing about the local process is claimed to contain hostile code.

the boundary Local process controls, timeouts, cancellation, bounded output, and redaction do not create hostile-code isolation. Autonomous execution is allowed only when the isolation evidence is materially stronger.

Then the differences are only in command shape and trimmed capability: Codex runs an ephemeral workspace-write sandbox inside the attempt worktree; Claude runs with acceptEdits so edits land but the human stays interruptible; Grok launches with subagents, memory, and web search disabled so its world matches the leaf; OMP can run supervised over RPC like the others. The footer boundary is the claim discipline: local process controls, timeouts, cancellation, bounded output, and redaction are operational conveniences — they do not create hostile-code isolation, and the deck never says otherwise. deep dive S57 · plate 57 of 66 · THE ADAPTERS — Human in the loop

Four adapters, one posture: a person is watching.

The mesh can drive four different executors, but all four share one posture — supervised execution, where a human may watch, interrupt, and accept. It is the default, and the only mode that needs no isolation proof.

The gold rail at the top is the equalizer: every adapter receives the same TaskHandoff/v3 — one authorized attempt per lane — and produces one observable attempt back. Nothing about the handoff changes with the executor; the authorized task is identical no matter who runs it. Preserving one handoff and one observable attempt is what keeps supervision meaningful: there is exactly one thing to watch.

What changes is command shape and trimmed capability. Codex runs an ephemeral workspace-write sandbox inside the attempt worktree. Claude runs with acceptEdits, so edits land but the human stays interruptible. Grok launches with subagents, memory, and web search disabled — its world trimmed to match the leaf. OMP can run supervised over RPC like the others.

Then the boundary, in red because it is a refusal: local process controls — timeouts, cancellation, bounded output, redaction — do not create hostile-code isolation. They are operational conveniences around code you decided to run, not a containment proof, and the deck never says otherwise. The claim stays precise because the next mode exists: whatever supervision cannot honestly cover, autonomous mode must prove. The capability trims are not arbitrary either — each adapter gives up exactly the capabilities the leaf never declared, so the executor's world matches the contract's world.

That is why this mode is called process separation: the attempt is separated from your session and your branch, observed and interruptible — and nothing stronger is claimed. If the executor cannot be trusted, watching is not enough — and pretending otherwise would be the silent downgrade the next page forbids.

How to read the plate
  • The gold rail is the shared handoff — TaskHandoff/v3, one attempt per lane.
  • The four cards differ only in command shape and trimmed capabilities.
  • The command snippets are the literal invocations — read them as the contract.
  • The red footer is the claim boundary — no hostile-code isolation here.
The boundary

Supervised mode promises observability and interruption, not containment. Untrusted execution needs autonomous mode — and autonomous mode needs verified isolation, priced on the next plate.

Isolate
the isolation · no silent downgrade

Autonomous mode fails closed without isolation.

Running without a supervisor is a different product posture, not a flag: autonomous OMP requires an explicitly verified container, route, model, capability, and a host-signed evidence chain. If any piece of that proof is missing or changed, the run refuses to start — it never quietly falls back to supervised semantics while claiming isolation.

no silent downgrade Downgrade is forbidden; missing proof fails closed. The most important isolation detail is what the worker never receives.

deep dive S58 · plate 58 of 66 · THE ISOLATION — No silent downgrade

Autonomy is priced in proof.

Removing the human from the loop is not a flag you set — it is a different product posture, earned with verified isolation or refused before the run starts. This page exists to keep the strongest word in the act honest.

Autonomous OMP requires an explicitly verified container, route, model, and capability, plus a host-signed evidence chain for the environment. Every link is checked before the attempt starts; the word autonomous is bought with proof, not with configuration.

The table prices the two postures side by side. Supervised adapters run as host processes; autonomous OMP runs in a Docker/Podman worker. Supervised requires a human watching; autonomous requires verified isolation instead. Supervised uses local provider access; autonomous gets an expiring attempt capability. Supervised makes no hostile-code claim; autonomous hardens to non-root, a read-only root filesystem, and dropped capabilities. And where supervised acceptance is plain Task-Spec POST, autonomous acceptance must additionally carry sandbox and environment evidence.

The red chips are the stable refusals: missing runtime, unverified proxy, image digest mismatch, missing model, changed evidence. Each one fails the run closed — before it starts — with a reason you can grep. Stability matters here: the same missing piece produces the same refusal every time, so automation can react to it. Changed evidence deserves a pause: if the evidence chain differs from what was verified — the pinned Dockerfile, the locked image — the run refuses rather than reconcile. The Dockerfile and image lock are part of that chain; the environment is pinned and hashed before a single token is spent.

What the system will never do is silently downgrade: incomplete isolation proof does not get you supervised execution dressed as autonomy — it gets you a refusal. And even at its strongest, the claim stays precise: host-signed environment evidence, not a container that proves everything.

How to read the plate
  • The five rows are the price list — process, supervisor, credentials, hardening, evidence.
  • The left column is supervised — honest about its limits.
  • The right column is autonomous — every convenience replaced by a verification.
  • The red chips are the fail-closed refusals — any one stops the run.
Why this page exists

Autonomous execution is permitted only when the isolation evidence is materially stronger — and the evidence is checked, not assumed. A missing check is a named refusal, never a quieter mode.

Least
the credential lease · least authority

The worker gets one capability — never the keyring.

Everything sensitive stays on the host side of the boundary: provider credentials, signing keys, evaluator keys, the SSH agent, the Docker socket, the home directory. Exactly one thin rail crosses — an expiring capability for one provider route, issued per attempt and revoked by time.

one writable workspace internal network → proxy only 1 CPU 512 MB 128 PIDs 64 MB tmpfs no-new-privileges known-secret redaction bounded output
least authority by default The boundary is drawn around secrets, not around convenience. The cockpit can disappear because authority and history live elsewhere.

The dashed red host card holds everything sensitive — provider credentials, signing keys, evaluator keys, the SSH agent, the Docker socket, the home directory — and it is labeled as never entering the worker. The cyan worker on the right is the attempt's whole world: one writable workspace, read-only everything else, network only to the proxy. deep dive S59 · plate 59 of 66 · THE CREDENTIAL LEASE — Least authority

The keyring never crosses.

The deepest isolation detail on this page is not a wall — it is the list of things that never enter the worker at all, and the one thin exception that proves the rule.

The dashed red card is the host side of the boundary, holding everything sensitive: provider credentials, signing keys, evaluator keys, the SSH agent, the Docker socket, the home directory. Read it as an inventory of what an attempt must never touch. Nothing on that list is copied, mounted, or forwarded — the boundary is drawn around secrets, not around convenience.

Exactly one rail crosses. The worker receives one expiring capability for one provider route — a CredentialLease issued per attempt, held by the proxy, revoked by time. The worker can call its model through that route and do nothing else with anyone's credentials; when the attempt ends, the capability dies with it. One route, one expiry, one attempt — the lease cannot be widened from inside the worker. This is least authority expressed as a physical fact: you cannot leak what you never received.

The cyan card is the attempt's whole world: one writable workspace, everything else read-only, a network that reaches the proxy and nothing else. The chips enumerate the rest of the budget — 1 CPU, 512 MB, 128 PIDs, 64 MB tmpfs, no-new-privileges, known-secret redaction, bounded output. Every limit is numeric and checkable, which is what makes the environment evidence host-signable.

Keep the promise scoped: this is least authority by default plus host-signed environment evidence — bounded container controls, precisely enumerated. The claim is not that the container proves everything; it is that the secrets were never in the room. That is why the next page can let the cockpit disappear: authority and history never lived there either.

How to read the plate
  • The dashed host card is the never-cross list — six kinds of sensitive material.
  • The single cyan rail is the only crossing — one expiring capability, one provider route.
  • The worker card is the attempt's whole world — one writable mount, proxy-only network.
  • The chips are the numeric budget — CPU, memory, PIDs, tmpfs, privileges, output.
Key detail

The capability pattern replaces credential copying with a scoped, expiring yes — everything else is a structural no. Least authority is enforced by absence, not by policy prose.

Cockpit
the cockpit · observe, control, hand back

Any cockpit can reconnect; only a human finishes.

The CLI and the local MCP are stateless windows over the same durable run: one cockpit can disconnect and another can reattach to identical state. And when the run is done, finish prints the human merge route — commands for a person to run — never an automatic target merge.

frontier→ explain→ start→ get / watch→ cancel / resume→ supervised accept→ finish
final screen · taskspec mesh finish run-42
# finish prints the human merge route — it never merges accepted work is on taskspec-mesh/run-42 · target branch untouched $ git checkout main $ git merge --no-ff taskspec-mesh/run-42
the MCP boundary
MCP is a local, stateless cockpit over the daemon — it reads the same events and issues the same requests. It cannot bypass leases or canonical acceptance; there is no privileged path through it.
observe · control · hand back The control plane ends where it began — with a person. That runtime sits behind a much broader — but still phase-oriented — CLI.
Story: the act closes by returning power to the human. On the canvas: the Codex cockpit detaches — the dashed rail stops short of the event line and nothing is lost — and the Claude cockpit reattaches to the same durable line, the same run-42, the same attempt B in verifying. The tool rail is the whole cockpit surface in order: frontier, explain, start, get and watch, cancel and resume, supervised accept, finish. Then the two callouts carry the closing boundaries: finish prints the merge commands — a human merge route, never an automatic target merge — and MCP is a local, stateless cockpit over the daemon that cannot bypass leases or canonical acceptance. That is the TaskMesh promise in one line: coordination without authority. deep dive S60 · plate 60 of 66 · THE COCKPIT — Observe, control, hand back

The window closes. The run doesn't.

A cockpit is only a window over the daemon's durable run — this closing page shows one window being swapped mid-run, and the one step the system always hands back to a person.

On the canvas, the Codex cockpit detaches — its dashed rail stops short of the event line, and nothing is lost, because nothing lived in the window. The Claude cockpit reattaches to the same durable event line: same run-42, same attempt B, same verifying state, replayed from the log. Any cockpit works, because the state never belonged to any of them. This is the payoff of every earlier page: because authority and history live in the daemon and its log, the cockpit is free to be disposable.

The chip rail is the whole cockpit surface in lifecycle order: frontier → explain → start → get / watch → cancel / resume → supervised accept → finish. Observe, control, hand back — the CLI and the local MCP expose the same durable run through the same requests. Each chip is one command; there is no hidden second interface.

The final screen is the one that matters most: when the run completes, finish prints the merge commands — the exact, safe route from taskspec-mesh/run-42 to the target branch. A human merge route: the screen shows commands for a person to run, never a confirmation that the mesh merged anything. Printing, not performing, is the whole point.

And the boundary for the newest cockpit: MCP is a local, stateless cockpit over the daemon. It reads the same events and issues the same requests; it cannot bypass leases or canonical acceptance. There is no privileged path through it — coordination without authority, to the very end. The act ends where it began: with power returned to the person.

How to read the plate
  • The greyed window is the disconnecting cockpit — closed, and nothing lost.
  • The solid cyan rail is the reconnect — same line, same run ID, replayed state.
  • The gold dot is run-42 on the durable event line — the run lives there.
  • The final screen shows merge commands — a human merge route, never an automatic merge.
Why this page exists

The act closes by returning power to the human: cockpits observe and control, the daemon remembers, canonical acceptance gates — and only a person finishes the target merge.

the cli · commands by phase

Forty-one commands, one lifecycle.

deep dive S61 · plate 61 of 66 · THE CLI — Commands by phase

A wide surface with a short daily route.

Every command the product ships is on this plate, sorted by the phase of the lifecycle it serves — and the sorting is the point: forty-one commands collapse into a six-verb routine you actually use every day.

Most tools hide their lifecycle behind flags and convention; you discover the surface by accident. Task-Spec makes each phase explicit instead — prepare the world, author leaves, seal authority at PRE, execute the attempt and accept the proof at POST, then evidence, graph, and runtime support. The seven lanes are this book's acts rendered as a command inventory: contracts, evidence, graph, runtime, and maintenance each get a lane because each is real, auditable surface rather than implicit magic — each phase can be run, scripted, and audited on its own, so nothing important happens offstage.

The everyday path stays short: plan decomposes intent into bounded leaves, validate checks the contract's shape, dod previews the definition of done, gate runs the PRE checks, handoff seals the attempt into a portable packet, and accept runs the independent POST verification. Everything else — holdout, receipt, bridge, mesh — is opt-in depth you reach for when a specific question needs evidence, never required ceremony.

The footer is the automation contract. --json makes every answer machine-readable, and --dry-run previews effects before they happen. Four exit codes let scripts branch without parsing prose: 0 success; 1 a contract or gate failure — a refusal, the system saying no on purpose; 2 a usage error; 3 the runtime floor, meaning the environment itself broke. A pipeline can tell “the gate refused” apart from “the tool crashed” — exactly the distinction a trust system must never blur.

One connection forward: the identity these commands create and seal is not trapped inside the CLI. It can cross protocol and packaging boundaries intact — which is the next plate.

How to read the plate
  • The seven lanes are lifecycle phases in the order work actually happens; lane colors echo the book's acts — gold for PRE authority, green for execute/accept.
  • Command chips are the CLI's real verbs; the dense lanes (evidence/interop, graph/backlog) are depth, not daily ceremony.
  • The footer strip is the scripting contract: global flags plus four exit codes, so a refusal (1) never reads as a crash (3).
Why this page exists

A contract system that hides its surface forces users to guess what exists. Publishing all forty-one commands by phase is the honest alternative: you see everything the product can do, and you see that an ordinary day needs only six of them.

deep dive S62 · plate 62 of 66 · THE ECOSYSTEM — Bridges and install doors

One identity, many doors — and no door mints authority.

Portability means the packet sealed in one tool still means exactly the same thing inside another — this plate shows the four crossings Task-Spec ships, and the honest limit stamped on every one of them.

At the center sits the portable identity: TaskHandoff/v3 plus its ReceiptSubject — the revision, the attempt id, and the acceptance digest. That triple is enough for any conformant consumer to know which authorized attempt a result belongs to, without phoning home to the CLI that produced it. It is what makes the handoff more than a file format: a packet other ecosystems can carry without reinterpretation.

Four rails carry that identity outward. An A2A artifact lets the attempt cross agent-to-agent boundaries intact. The MCP task/tool surface opens a local cockpit with the same contracts and the same refusals. A DSSE/in-toto envelope signs the receipt into a standard attestation wrapper that supply-chain tooling already understands. And harness skills — Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Cursor, Kimi — put the same contract where agents actually run.

The sentence under the center plate is the whole doctrine: identity survives the crossing — authority does not move. A bridge can carry the record of what was authorized and what was accepted; it cannot grant new scope. So the Claude plugin is a skill entry, not a second contract, and pinned A2A/MCP conformance is evidence about tested versions — never an ecosystem-wide certification of everything that claims the protocol.

Below the diagram, four install doors meet different trust postures: a source checkout, a pinned private release archive, npm plus a Git tag, and the Claude plugin skill entry. Adoption is a choice of door; the contract behind every door is the same one, and none of the doors asks you to trust a fork of the format. The doors differ in packaging, never in contract.

How to read the plate
  • The center plate is the portable identity — revision, attempt id, acceptance digest: the triple that survives every crossing.
  • Cyan rails are protocol bridges — A2A, MCP, DSSE/in-toto; the purple destination is harness skills: five harnesses, one contract.
  • The install strip is the way in: source checkout, pinned private archive, npm + Git tag, Claude plugin skill entry.
  • The red tag is the boundary — pinned conformance is evidence, not ecosystem certification.
The boundary

A bridge transports proof; it never manufactures it. Nothing on this plate grants authority that a PRE gate did not seal first — portability moves identity, never permission.

Dogfood
the dogfood · the product built its own leaves

Task-Spec dogfoods Task-Spec.

The strongest argument is not a benchmark — it is the repository itself. Approved release manifests decomposed 3.8.1 and TaskMesh 3.9.0 into accepted leaves and parked composition nodes: the same contracts, gates, and receipts from this deck, pointed inward at the product.

The approved TaskMesh 3.9.0 release manifest decomposed the program into eight accepted leaves — contracts and CLI, daemon and state, leases and graph, routes and worktrees, supervised adapters, autonomous isolation, cockpit and MCP, package and release — and every one of them flows into a single XXL composition node that stays dashed and parked, because XXL is never executed as a leaf; it decomposes. The receipt detail on the right is a real accepted-task frontmatter, sanitized: the tier, one attempt id, the authorization reference redacted, and the acceptance-record digest redacted — the qualifier is that authorization and acceptance refs are shown as shapes, never as live HMAC or digest values. deep dive S63 · plate 63 of 66 · THE DOGFOOD — The product built its own leaves

The product shipped itself through its own gates.

Dogfooding means the repository's own releases were decomposed, authorized, executed, and accepted with the very contracts this book describes — the methodology's strongest evidence is the repo you are already reading.

The approved TaskMesh 3.9.0 manifest decomposed the release program into eight leaves: contracts and CLI, daemon and state, leases and graph, routes and worktrees, supervised adapters, autonomous isolation, cockpit and MCP, package and release. Each leaf is a bounded task — one attempt, one receipt — and each was accepted through the same PRE and POST gates any user task would face. Green chips, not promises — and the full text of each leaf is in the repo.

The dashed gold frame is a composition node — the XXL node holding the whole program. The terminology is load-bearing: leaves (XS through L) execute; composition nodes (XL and XXL) never execute — they decompose. So the frame stays parked: the parent of the eight accepted leaves in the plan, not a mega-task an agent ran in one heroic shot. Parked is a status, not a failure: the program was fully decomposed, so the XXL node has no work left to do as a task.

The right panel is the receipt detail — sanitized frontmatter from one accepted task. tier: 1, Tier 1 eligible. One attempt_id. An authorization_ref, the sealed PRE authority, redacted. An acceptance_record digest, the POST receipt, redacted. The chain of authority stays visible as shapes without exposing live key material — authorization sealed before work, acceptance recorded after it, and never one word for both.

Why this matters: claims about a methodology are cheap, and benchmarks can be cherry-picked. Repository evidence cannot. tasks/.plans/, tasks/done/, and .taskspec/acceptance/ are rereadable proof that the product's own construction obeyed the discipline it asks of its users. A skeptical reviewer does not have to believe this book; they can open the directory.

How to read the plate
  • Eight green chips are the accepted leaves; the rails roll each leaf up to its parent.
  • The dashed gold frame is the parked XXL composition node — present in the plan, never executed in a worktree.
  • The right panel is sanitized accepted-task frontmatter: tier, attempt id, authorization ref, acceptance digest.
  • Redacted refs are shapes, not secrets — the authority chain is inspectable without live key material.
Key detail

Authorization and acceptance are different moments with different records — sealed before the work, recorded after it. The frontmatter keeps both side by side under one attempt id, which is what makes the leaf self-explanatory.

deep dive S64 · plate 64 of 66 · THE EVOLUTION — From format to control plane

A history of things that became provable.

Read this timeline as a trust chain, not a changelog: each milestone made one more property of the system explicit and checkable — what used to be implied became evidence — while older formats stayed readable the whole way.

v3 fixed the six-zone atomic contract and closed the PRE/POST loop — authority sealed before work, acceptance independent after it. 3.6 bound the handoff to one exact sealed revision and built the acceptance experience: from then on, an attempt carries its authority with it, and a mutated contract is detectable rather than debatable. Six milestones carry the arc; not every patch release earns a node.

3.7 laid the v4 evidence foundations — holdouts, identities, environment, interop — so the system records where and as whom an attempt ran, not just what it claimed. 3.8.1 hardened the product with real-engine, sandbox, and protocol evidence, scored once under the fixed 97/100 corridor. 3.9.0 added the optional TaskMesh layer — a local control plane over already-authorized leaves, not a hosted service and never an authorizer. Each of those surfaces was a place the product previously said “trust us.”

The last node is dashed on purpose. Current main carries roster and repository-organization work implemented at the audited HEAD — real, but explicitly not frozen 3.9 proof. The book labels that difference instead of quietly folding new work into old evidence, and releases keep formats 1–4 readable rather than rewriting history. Readable history is itself a trust surface: a format-1 file from the beginning still parses today.

The reading rule this page teaches: a trust chain is credible only when every link states what it added and what it still refuses to claim. Milestones that merely add features do not belong on this spine. That is why the next plate splits the proof into two corridors and lets each one state its own boundary.

How to read the plate
  • The gold spine is release order; the alternating cards are story beats — six milestones, not every patch release.
  • Node colors mark what each link added: gold the contract, cyan the evidence layer, green the hardening corridor, purple the control plane.
  • The dashed amber node is current main — implemented and audited at HEAD, never frozen release proof.
Why this page exists

Without the timeline, the two evidence corridors on the next plate read as a contradiction. With it, they read as what they are: successive tightenings of one proof boundary at a time.

deep dive S65 · plate 65 of 66 · THE PROOF — Released vs current

Two frozen scorecards and one live audit.

Evidence is trustworthy only when it says exactly which question it answers — this plate keeps two frozen release corridors apart and lets current main speak for itself, drift included.

The 3.8.1 corridor answers “how strong was the product at release?” A fixed rubric scored it once — 97/100 across authority, lifecycle, docs, packaging, engines, protocol pins, and the signed sandbox — and froze the result as release evidence. Frozen means it never moves: history you can re-read, not a live dashboard that quietly updates itself. Seven surfaces, one number, no moving goalposts.

Three of the hundred points were deliberately unavailable: universal semantic truth, ecosystem-wide certification, and long-running production reliability. A contract system can make scope, authority, and proof checkable; it cannot honestly promise those three — so the rubric refuses to score them rather than grading on vibes. That refusal is the difference between a quality score and marketing copy.

The 3.9.0 corridor answers a different question: “does the optional TaskMesh local control plane work as evidenced?” — local and hosted conformance, live isolation, install, recovery, cockpit, private provenance and publication. Its refusal list matters just as much: no hosted control plane, no production-reliability claim, no protocol certification, no Tier 1 straight from worktrees, no automatic target merge — the human merge route stays human. Each retained artifact is named in the evidence file, and each refusal is printed next to it — the corridor is as proud of what it excludes as of what it includes.

The narrow amber strip is current main, audited 2026-08-26: the most exact make check suites revalidated, and the final gate currently fails on missing README release-status markers — RELEASE_STATUS=STALE. That is documentation projection drift, named on the plate — not hidden, and not a reason to rewrite the frozen evidence. Two corridors, two questions, one habit: read the boundary before the score.

How to read the plate
  • The two big cards are frozen corridors — each states its question, its score, and its honest boundary.
  • Red text is the refusal list: claims the evidence explicitly does not make.
  • The amber strip is the live audit of current main — revalidated suites plus one known drift, named.
  • Frozen vs audited is the axis: release evidence never changes; main is re-checked and allowed to drift in daylight.
Key detail

Released evidence is immutable; current main is audited, not frozen. Collapsing the two would make both worthless — you would no longer know which question any number answers.
